answer:K21-cpp-overloads.cost: None: decided when compiling. Each call is a direct call to the thunk of the chosen declaration, the same call C++ makes to that overload. There is no table, no dispatch and nothing checked while the program runs.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 125: C++ members stay unsafe until an overlay entry vouches
verdicts_kept.how: Kept per declaration. An overload with no entry stays unsafe to call. An entry written `unsafe fn` carries its own `@safety` for its one declaration, which the FFI-12 sentence guarantees, so one line never vouches for a declaration its writer did not name.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 131: C++ member lines go under their class
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. Entries for overloaded members (`fn new(width, height)`, `fn set_volume(level: f32)`) go under their `class` section. A top-level entry still names only a function outside any class, and one naming only members is still `E5010`.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 132: @ffi(const) on an entry
verdicts_kept.how: Kept per declaration. Each overload's method entry means what it says: without `@ffi(const)` that method changes its object, with it the method only reads. Overloads of one name may differ in this, and each entry says it of the one declaration it describes.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 146 and 147: `owns` at a call only for an `owns` parameter, and always there
verdicts_kept.how: Kept and used. Because the words at the call count, `push(item)` and `push(owns item)` pick `const T&` and `T&&` respectively. With only one of the two declared, the existing errors stay as they are (E3028, and verdict 146's 'remove `owns`').

verdicts_kept.verdict: 134: one L3015 per C or C++ function, naming every other call
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, with each declaration of an overloaded name counted as one function. This is listed in to_verify.

decisions.title: How a C++ name declared several times reaches Ember
decisions.problem: C++ headers declare several constructors and overloaded methods and functions under one name, but Ember's own declarations have no overloading. The spec does not say what Ember names they get or how a call picks one. The compiler can work out which declaration a call means from its arguments. Only when two fit equally does it need a written word (`x as T`) or a refusal.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)   # Renderer(int, int)
r.draw(mesh)                           # draw(const Mesh&)
r.draw(hud)                            # draw(const Sprite&)
options.outcome: Compiles and calls the declaration the arguments fit: count, words at the call, then types, exact before coercion. A call that fits none is `E2020` and one that fits two equally is `E2070`, each naming every declaration.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)
r.draw_Mesh(mesh)
r.draw_Sprite(hud)
options.outcome: Compiles. Each overload is its own Ember function, named from types the program never wrote; the names change when the header renames a type.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "renderer.hpp":
    class Renderer:
        rename new(width, height) as sized
        rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh
        rename draw(sprite) as draw_sprite
# then: r = eng.gfx.Renderer.sized(1280, 720); r.draw_mesh(mesh)
options.outcome: Without the overlay, every overload is skipped and `r.draw(mesh)` is the 'skipped: overloaded' diagnostic. With it, the renamed calls compile, at the cost of a new `rename` form and one overlay line per overload.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. Speed is equal for all three options: a direct thunk call chosen when compiling. Safety is equal too: every mistake is refused when compiling. On readability A reads as the header and as a call in Python; B's invented names read worst; C makes the ordinary import longer. 2. Safety (C4): A refuses a call that two declarations fit equally, so nothing is picked silently. 3. Compile time first (C5): all three are compile time. 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): the compiler can work out the declaration from the arguments; B and C make the programmer read or write bookkeeping names. 5. The ordinary program (C2): A leaves it as written; C adds overlay lines to every C++ import with overloads. 6. Consistency (C6): FFI-39b already selects a C++ constructor by arity and argument types, and TYP-24 already tells instances apart by a call's arguments in the same order. TYP-26's exception gives its reason (principle 6): the header, not the program, declares the functions.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: No verdict covers C++ overloads, so none is departed from. The choice narrows §I.6's non-goal 'function overloading' to Ember's own declarations, as TYP-26's existing exceptions already do for operator-interface implementations. It is recorded for the owner's later review.

owner_short.one_line: A C++ class with two constructors and two `draw(...)` overloads: what Ember calls them, and how a call picks one.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | header | declares `Renderer()`, `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)`, `draw(const Sprite&)` | four functions, two names |
| 2 | importer | keeps one Ember name per C++ name | `Renderer.new`, `r.draw` |
| 3 | compiler | at `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` picks the one the arguments fit (count, `ref mut`/`owns` at the call, types) | `Renderer(int, int)` |
| 4 | compiler | at `r.draw(hud)` picks by type | `draw(const Sprite&)` |
| 5 | compiler | a call two of them fit equally | refused when compiling, naming both |
owner_short.today: The spec does not say: Ember's 'no two functions of one name' rule, the 'skip what cannot be imported' rule and the base-constructor pick each give a different answer.
options: A: one Ember name per C++ name, and the call picks by its arguments: `Renderer.new(1280, 720)`, `r.draw(mesh)`
B: one name per overload, built from its types: `Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)`, `r.draw_Mesh(mesh)`
C: overloads are skipped until an overlay renames each one: `rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh`, then `r.draw_mesh(mesh)`
owner_short.recommendation: A: the code reads the way the header does, nothing extra is written, and it is how a class with a C++ base already picks its base constructor.

decisions.title: How an overlay entry names one of several declarations that share name, count and parameter names
decisions.problem: Overlay entries are matched by name, parameter count and parameter names. `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)` share all three, so an entry cannot say which one it vouches for. The compiler cannot know which declaration the writer meant, so only a written word or a refusal remain.

options.outcome: Each entry describes exactly one declaration. `fn set_volume(level)` fits both and is `E5010`, naming both. If the header later adds an overload that an entry then fits, the build stops at that entry.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "mixer.hpp":
    extend Mixer:
        fn set_volume_f(level: f32):
            # SAFETY: set_volume(float) only stores the level
            unsafe:
                this.set_volume(level)
options.outcome: No entry can name either overload, so `fn set_volume(level)` is `E5010` and both stay unsafe to call. Vouching needs a wrapper with an invented name.
The entry makes both overloads safe. If the header later adds `set_volume(void* level)`, the package's own build adds its record line and the new overload is vouched for without anyone reading it.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once: (c) fails safety. 2. Safety (C4): (a) and (b) vouch only for what is written; (c) lets an unread declaration become safe to call. 3. Compile time (C5): all three. 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): the type in (a) says which declaration the entry's facts are about, which is the entry's meaning; (b) forces a bookkeeping wrapper with an invented name. 5. The ordinary program (C2): (a) changes no line where count or names already tell overloads apart, and adds one type only where they do not. 6. Consistency (C6): Ember writes a parameter's type as `name: Type`, and an `@ffi(macro_fn)` entry already writes types this way. Checklist 12 says to add the missing syntax rather than exempt the case.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: None. It keeps verdicts 125, 131 and 132 per declaration. It departs from one lead ruling, not a verdict: §10 of decisions.md dropped types from class entries to keep 'one way to write an overlay line'. Here the type returns only where the names cannot single out one declaration, in the form macro_fn entries already use.

owner_short.one_line: One overlay line for one of two C++ overloads that share their parameter name: `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)`.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | header | declares `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)` | same name, same count, same parameter name |
| 2 | overlay writer | writes `fn set_volume(level: f32)` and `fn set_volume(level: c_int)` | each line names one |
| 3 | compiler | checks each line against the header | each overload safe to call as its own line says |
| 4 | overlay writer | writes `fn set_volume(level)` instead | refused: it fits both, and the error names them |
| 5 | header, later | adds `set_volume(double level)` | any line that now fits two stops the build |
owner_short.today: An overlay line is matched only by name, parameter count and parameter names, so no line can name one of these two overloads.
options: a: the line writes the parameter's type the way Ember shows it: `fn set_volume(level: f32)`
b: no line can name one, so both stay unsafe to call unless a wrapper with a new name is written in the overlay
c: `fn set_volume(level)` covers both, and also covers any overload the header adds later, without anyone checking it
owner_short.recommendation: a: one extra word, only where the names cannot tell the overloads apart, and nothing is vouched for without being written.

to_verify: Today's compiler on the J8-04 program with no overlay: what it does with two `new` and two `draw`. Does it give E1030, pick one by name, or skip them? decisions.md item 19 says entries are found by name.

After the edit: `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` runs `Renderer(int, int)`, `r.draw(mesh)` runs `draw(const Mesh&)` and `r.draw(hud)` runs `draw(const Sprite&)`. Check each with a print on the C++ side, on the LLVM backend (Clang) and on the C backend with MSVC and Clang.
Words at the call pick: `q.push(first)` runs `push(const Job&)`, `q.push(owns second)` runs `push(Job&&)`, and a later use of `second` is E3040.

An imported constructor `X.new(owns n)` for a `T&&` parameter is an ordinary call: call words apply (verdict 147), not verdict 159's no-word rule for `Name(args)` constructors. Otherwise `Widget(const Name&)` and `Widget(Name&&)` would fit equally.
Literal ranking follows TYP-24: `js.json.Value.new(3)` picks `long long`, `new(0.5)` picks `double` and `new(true)` picks `bool`.

`E2070` naming both declarations for a call two fit equally: Linux `seek(long)` and `seek(long long)` both `i64`, and a declaration with C++ default arguments beside one without them. `E2020` naming every declaration for a call that fits none.

Overlay: `fn set_volume(level: f32)` and `fn set_volume(level: c_int)` each match one declaration. `fn set_volume(level)` is E5010 naming both. A header that adds a third `set_volume` with parameter `level` makes an untyped entry E5010 on the next build. Types written with contract words also parse, e.g. `fn fill(data: *mut c_int borrowed one)`.
`super.init(…)` on an Ember class with a C++ base still picks the same declaration under the general sentence as under FFI-39b's first sentence.
Verdict 134's L3015 counts each declaration of an overloaded name as one function, with every other call listed. Verdict 132's `@ffi(const)` is applied per overload entry.
`ember.overlays` (FFI-55) keys each described declaration so that overloads of one name get separate lines.
`ember bind --init` writes a type into starter entries exactly where count and names are shared, and the starter compiles unchanged.
`hide draw` and `rename draw as render` act on every declaration of the name.
An overlay `extend` block method with the same name as a header method is still E1030.
answer:K21-cpp-overloads.notes:
Process slip: before re-reading rule G, I ran `wc -l` once on JOB.md and decisions.md to get their lengths. Nothing else was run, and nothing was written or changed.

Why not already_decided: no line decides the case. TYP-26 would make the overloads E1030, FFI-20a would skip them, and FFI-39b picks only at `super.init`. FFI-48's row implies that overloads differing in parameter types import, but does not say how. The finder's option A left a hole: overloads with the same parameter count and names (`set(int value)`, `set(float value)`, very common) cannot be named by an entry. Decision 2 closes it.

Left for K47 (J8-05): the receiver-const pair (`T& at(i)` / `const T& at(i) const`) has identical parameters. FFI-48's row refuses it where the results differ; otherwise a call is E2070 under these words. FFI-48's 'rename one in the overlay' cannot name one declaration. That is pre-existing: `rename` takes a name, which is every declaration of it, today as after this change.

For the lead (codes and tooling, not language): E2070's row in the code table reads 'ambiguous interface method' and should also cover ambiguous C++ calls. FFI-55's record keys need to tell overloads apart. §I.6's non-goal 'function overloading' stays true of Ember's own declarations, but could say so ('of its own'); I.6 is not an allowed rule here.

Ember's literal defaults can pick a different overload than C++ would for the same literal: with `set(int)` and `set(long long)`, `set(5)` picks `long long` because Ember's `int` is 64 bits. A typed argument picks the other. Overload sets share a meaning, so the program's intent holds.

Overloads that import as the same Ember types on one target (Linux `long` and `long long`) are E2070 at every call there and compile on Windows. That comes from C's per-target aliases (FFI-8 already calls `c_wchar` not portable); the way out is a C++-side wrapper.

answer:K31-c-kept-callback-declaration.intent: A game gives a C event library a function that C keeps and runs during later `poll_events()` calls, adding a point each time. A token ends the registration. The danger in C++ terms: a `void*` user-data pointer to a lambda that has already gone out of scope (use after free).

existing_rule.rule: FFI-21, with FFI-10 (and FFI-11's ownership row, FN-2a)
existing_rule.words: FFI-21 402-405: "the function value, its code and its state, is moved into a block of its own, and C is given the trampoline as the function pointer and the block's tagged number as the user data"; 408: "With `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` C keeps the function after the call"; 415: "`retained` returns a `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token". FFI-10 79-81: "A `safe fn` writes the safe Ember types and the words in front of its parameters' names (`ref mut`, `owns`) produced by those words"; 82-84: "complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`"; 86-88: "The contract marks it as an ABI witness: it is absent from the callable Ember signature, and the compiler supplies the corresponding ... length at the call". FFI-11 290: "C keeps Ember memory only when it is handed over (`owns`)". FN-2a 115-122: "A call says ... `owns` before one it takes over ... whatever is given ... a function written in the call is given the same way".

edits.before:
C is given the trampoline as the function pointer and the block's tagged
  number as the user data. With `callback(borrowed)` C runs the function only during the call, the
  block is freed when the call returns, and the function may use the caller's real variables, as a
  function given to any call that runs it then may (Part VI), within `[FFI-22]`'s thread rule. With
  `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` C keeps the function after the call: its capture list says
  what it holds (`owns`, `copy of`, `thread_shared`; `shares`, `shares mut` and `weakref` only under
  `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)`, `[FFI-22]`), and a name it uses with no word is `E7004`: "C
  keeps this function after `setup` returns (`callback(retained)`), so it cannot use `setup`'s `game`;
  say what it holds: write `return register_cb(fn() owns game: game.add_point())` in place of line 17
edits.after:
C is given the trampoline as the function pointer and the block's tagged
  number as the user data. The parameter's Ember type is then a function value whose parameters and
  result are the C callback's, less the callback parameter that receives the user data, and the
  registering function's user-data parameter leaves the callable signature (`[FFI-10]`). With
  `callback(borrowed)` C runs the function only during the call, the
  block is freed when the call returns, and the function may use the caller's real variables, as a
  function given to any call that runs it then may (Part VI), within `[FFI-22]`'s thread rule. With
  `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` C keeps the function after the call, so it is handed over,
  as everything Ember gives C to keep is (`[FFI-11]`): the parameter is written `owns` and the call
  says `owns` before the function (`[FN-2a]`); its capture list says
  what it holds (`owns`, `copy of`, `thread_shared`; `shares`, `shares mut` and `weakref` only under
  `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)`, `[FFI-22]`), and a name it uses with no word is `E7004`: "C
  keeps this function after `setup` returns (`callback(retained)`), so it cannot use `setup`'s `game`;
  say what it holds: write `return register_cb(owns fn() owns game: game.add_point())` in place of line 17
edits.why_general: The new words state two properties the rule already has. (1) A callback with user data is a function value whose user-data argument the compiler fills (402-405 and 420: "an `Option` of a function value"). So its Ember type is the C callback's signature without that parameter, and the registering function's user-data parameter is not the program's to pass, which is what FFI-11 already says of a `count(n)` length. (2) What C keeps after the call leaves the caller ("moved into a block", FFI-11: "C keeps Ember memory only when it is handed over"). The language writes a hand-over as `owns` on the parameter and at the call, for every type (FN-1, FN-2a, verdicts 84, 147). The words name no type, signature or library, so they decide every kept callback: `retained` or `once`; any thread contract (FFI-22 then adds `thread_shared`); any C callback signature; nullable (an `Option` of it); a hand declaration or an overlay entry (FFI-11's vocabulary is shared); a function written in the call or taken from a variable. The E7004 line is the same property applied to the spec's own suggested line, which must compile (verdict 73).

edits.before:
An unsafe raw-pointer declaration keeps its written C ABI parameters; only a mapped `safe fn`
  erases the witness.
edits.after: A callback's `user_data=p` makes `p` such a witness too: it is written with its C type at its C ABI position, the compiler passes the callback block's tagged number there (`[FFI-21]`), and, since it is never exposed, its raw pointer is no `E5002`.
edits.why_general: FFI-10's witness property (ODR-074) is this: a parameter whose argument the compiler supplies at the call is written at its C ABI position and is absent from the callable signature. FFI-21 already makes the user-data argument the compiler's (the block's tagged number), and no program could supply it, so the property reaches it. The raw-pointer `E5002` exists because complete facts do not make a raw pointer "safe to expose". A witness is never exposed, so the ban does not reach it. This holds for every hand-declared user-data callback, whatever the user-data pointer's C type and position. It leaves `out` and `inout_count` carriers as FFI-10 leaves them.

No new rule: the spec's only hand declaration of a kept callback now follows its own rules. FFI-10 79-84: a `safe fn` writes the Ember types and words its contract produces, and no exposed raw pointer. FFI-21 as edited: a function value taken over with `owns`. FFI-10 as edited: `ud` is a witness. FFI-21 415: `retained` gives the token as the result. FN-2a: `owns` at the call. The example then shows the one spelling that every kept callback uses.

answers.question: J8-01
answers.today: Refused under the rules as written. Line 14 is `E5002` (FFI-10 82-84) because `ud: *mut void` is a raw-pointer parameter on a `safe fn`. Also, `cb` is written as the C carrier, not as the Ember type its contract words produce (79-81). Even if the declaration were accepted, line 18 would pass one argument where two are declared, pass a `fn()` where an `extern "C" fn(*mut void)` is declared, and return a token from a declaration that has no result. No words say what `cb`'s Ember type is, that `ud` leaves the call, or whether the call writes `owns`.
answers.after: As written, it is still refused, but now every error message gives the fix. Line 14: `E5002` names `cb`, because a callback with user data that C keeps is a function value taken over (`owns cb: fn()`), and names the result (`-> Retained[ForeignCallback]`). Line 18: `E3028` says `register_cb` takes the function over: `register_cb(owns fn() owns game: game.add_point())`. Written as the edited FFI-52 lines, it compiles: `safe fn register_cb(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]` and `return register_cb(owns fn() owns game: game.add_point())`. `setup` hands the function over, the compiler passes the block's tagged number as `ud`, and the call returns the token. Each time C runs the callback during `poll_events()`, it adds a point. `println(game.score)` prints how many times C ran it. `token`'s end calls `unregister`. Passing `ud` as well is too many arguments.
answers.decides: p16-ffi.md 404-412 (FFI-21 as edited: a function-value type, the user-data parameter leaves the callable signature, a kept function is handed over with `owns`); 91-92 (FFI-10 as edited: the user-data witness); 79-84 (FFI-10: a `safe fn` writes the Ember types and words its contract produces, and no exposed raw pointer); 415 (FFI-21: `retained` returns the token); p05-declarations.md 115-122 (FN-2a: `owns` before an argument the callee takes over, a function written in the call included)

sibling_cases.case: A server's metrics timer that C runs on its own thread, a callback with a parameter of its own (threads(any))
sibling_cases.program:
from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained
from std.sync import Atomic

class Stats:
    ticks: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `timer_start` was given")
    unsafe fn timer_cancel(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void, u32), ud: *mut void)
    # C calls `on_tick` from its timer thread with `ud` and the milliseconds elapsed
    @ffi(param(on_tick, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(any)), destroys(timer_cancel))
    safe fn timer_start(ms: u32, owns on_tick: thread_shared fn(u32), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn server_run_once()

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared Stats()
    timer = timer_start(250, owns fn(elapsed: u32) thread_shared stats: stats.ticks.fetch_add(1))
    server_run_once()
    println(stats.ticks.load())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. `on_tick`'s Ember type is the C callback `void (*)(void*, uint32_t)` less the parameter that receives the user data, so `fn(u32)`. FFI-22 makes it `thread_shared`. `ud` is filled by the compiler, and `timer`'s end cancels the timer. `timer_start(250, fn(elapsed: u32) thread_shared stats: ...)` without `owns` is `E3028`. Passing a third argument is too many arguments.

sibling_cases.case: A UI toolkit given a named function from a variable (threads(main))
sibling_cases.program:
from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Hud:
    frames: int = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `ui_on_frame` was given")
    unsafe fn ui_unwatch(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(main)), destroys(ui_unwatch))
    safe fn ui_on_frame(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn ui_run_frame()

fn main():
    hud = shares mut Hud()
    count_frame = fn() shares mut hud: hud.frames += 1
    watch = ui_on_frame(owns count_frame)
    ui_run_frame()
    println(hud.frames)
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. The named function is handed over and `count_frame` ends, so a later `count_frame()` is `E3040`. `ui_on_frame(count_frame)` is `E3028`. FN-2a's lent rule covers only standard-library functions that run a function during the call, and C keeps this one past the call.

sibling_cases.case: A diagnostics library imported from its header through an overlay entry (not a hand declaration)
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. The same contract words give the imported `log_set_sink` the signature `(owns sink: fn(c_int)) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]`, with `ud` absent from it (FFI-11's vocabulary is the overlay's). The call says `owns`. `sink`'s end calls `log_clear_sink`, and `log_flush()` may run the sink (FFI-52).

readability.verdict: Not harder, and only one word longer at the call. The declaration now says what Ember code gets: it takes a function over and gives back the token. The C plumbing type is gone from the Ember side, and `ud` stays where C has it, as a counted length's witness does. The call gains `owns`, the word every hand-over says (verdict 147, as in `thread.spawn(owns fn() ...)` and `widget_take(owns first)`). `main` is unchanged (`setup(shares mut game)`, verdict 160). The before did not compile at all.

answer:K31-c-kept-callback-declaration.cost: None: decided when compiling (the declaration's mapping and the call word). The run-time path is FFI-53's checked trampoline, which this edit does not change. FFI-53 states its cost as 1.02x to 1.05x of a C call through a function pointer; to measure only if the lead wants that figure re-checked.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 31: a C call may run the callbacks C keeps
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. Only the declaration and the call are spelled differently. The edited FFI-52 example still has `poll_events()` run the kept callback and `@ffi(no_callbacks) sqrt` run none.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 39 (now inferred, 86): what kept callbacks change
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. What the callback changes is still worked out from its body (FFI-52), and nothing is written for it.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 62: a callback that removes its own token stays alive until it finishes
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The token, the block and FFI-53's delayed free are untouched. The block still holds the handed-over function.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 91: into_raw only inside unsafe; a C function declared as keeping an object takes it by an ordinary hand-over
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, and the same property is used for functions. A function C keeps is given by an ordinary hand-over (`owns`), never with `into_raw()`.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 102: `owns` in a C contract
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The word for "C keeps this" on the Ember side is `owns`, as FFI-11 writes it for an object.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 114 fix 3: an object C keeps never moves
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The verdict is about class objects given to a `retained` pointer, and nothing about them changes. A callback's state lives in FFI-53's table, which never moves.

answer:K31-c-kept-callback-declaration.notes:
Reading the finder missed: much of this was already decided. FFI-10 79-84 already makes a `safe fn` write the Ember types and words its contract produces, and refuses an exposed raw pointer. So the example's `extern "C" fn(*mut void)` and `*mut void` on a `safe fn` were already `E5002`, and its result was already the token (FFI-21 415: "`retained` returns a `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token"). FN-2a already puts `owns` at the call for every `owns` parameter, and FFI-54 already does so for a foreign one (`widget_take(owns first)`). What was missing were words. FFI-21 never said which Ember type the callback parameter has, that what C keeps is handed over (`owns`), or that the user-data parameter leaves the call. FFI-10's witness words reached only `count(n)`. Those are the edits.

Knock-on outside the allowed rules: FFI-22's `E7015` message (p16-ffi.md 450) gives `return register_cb(fn() thread_shared game: game.add_point())`. After this edit that line needs `owns` before `fn()`. Messages are the lead's to word (JOB.md "Messages and tests").

New gaps, not caused by this edit:
- (1) A registering C function with a result of its own that `destroys(f)` takes ("the token keeps them", FFI-11 303-304). With the token as the call's result, the spec gives the C result's type no place in a hand declaration.
- (2) `callback(borrowed)`: FFI-21 says every user-data function is "moved into a block of its own", while FFI-11's `borrowed` is a view for the call. Whether a named function given to a borrowed C callback is lent (as standard-library functions lend it, verdict 150) or handed over is not said. This edit does not touch the borrowed case.
- (3) The Ember types of a C callback's own pointer parameters (their contracts) are not covered.

Left to K53: whether `callback(once)` gives a token, and whether its parameter may be a `once fn`. The new type words say only "a function value", so they decide neither. The `owns` hand-over for `once` follows from "C keeps the function after the call", the same as for `retained`. Consistent with the cluster note: a named function given to a kept-callback parameter takes `owns` (sibling 2).

answer:K06-sharing-a-local.intent: Keep using a local, and views of it, after giving it another owner (the shop's stock is the same inventory `g` reads); and hand settings finished on the main thread to a worker thread.

existing_rule.words: p08 107-108 [RC-1]: "a local of this function (which becomes one of the owners)". The local stays the same value as one of its owners. Nothing ends it, and BCK-4 (p18 185-186) names no storage end at a sharing line. p11 70-72 [THR-1]: "it is written before a new value (`st = thread_shared Stats()`) or on a value already `thread_shared` (`fn() thread_shared st:`), and on a value made otherwise it is `E7017`", and E7017's message (p11 72-74, p07 140-142) is written for a function's own object: "`names` is `share_and_keep`'s own object, which it may change; to share it between threads, create it shared".

edits.before: (`count = shares mut Counter()`, `other = shares items`), one allocation.
edits.after: Making a local shared moves nothing that points into it: the local stays the one value it was, now one of its owners (`[RC-1]`), and where something that points into it is used across the line that shares it, the compiler gives the local its block where the local begins, the same one allocation, made earlier.
edits.why_general: It says what sharing a local is: one more owner of the same value, and nothing moves under anything that points into it. It holds for every inline type (struct, enum, tuple, list, string), for every kind of pointer into a local (a view, a kept view, a position, a captured `ref`, a `sharedref mut` link) and on every path (a sharing line that runs only on some paths or more than once, a local declared in a loop or kept in a generator's frame). The compiler finds out when compiling which locals need the earlier block, so a program that compiles without this sentence pays nothing. A class object already has its block, so nothing of it moves. No refusal is added and no word is written.

edits.before: `shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a
edits.after: `thread_shared x` is written only before a new value or a value already `thread_shared` (`[THR-1]`, `E7017`), and `shares x` and `shares mut x` before a new value, a
edits.why_general: It puts into the rule on owners the property the rule on threads already gives the word: a value several threads own is made that way where it is made, with the header it keeps for life (OBJ-1), so no value that already exists becomes one. That holds for every type and for every place a value can come from (a local, a call's result, an `owns` parameter, a part), with no exception by type. It leaves `shares` and `shares mut` of a local (verdict 23) and E2122 for a one-owner place (verdict 103) as they are.

answer:K06-sharing-a-local.cost: J5-06: none for every program that compiles without the edit; its block is still made at the sharing line. Where something pointing into a local is used across that line, the same one allocation is made where the local begins (C: one malloc for a value it shares through a counted pointer). Two costs to measure: on a path that never reaches the sharing line, that allocation and its free are paid where they would not otherwise be; and before that line the local's fields are reached through the block's address, not the frame. J4-05: none: decided when compiling.

decisions.title: A view of a local survives the line that makes the local shared (J5-06)
decisions.problem: HEAP-3 puts a local's value in a block at the line that shares it, and no rule says whether a view taken before that line still points into it. Read word for word, `println(g)` reads the frame slot `inv` left. No rule as written ends a view at a sharing line: BCK-4's storage ends, VII.1's "handed over" (the giver's name ends, and `inv`'s does not) and VII.1's "reshape" all leave it out. So the existing rules accept the program, and HEAP-3's placement words had to say how that stays safe.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: B keeps C's speed (the same one allocation), safety (the view points into the block) and the program as written; A gives up readability and gains nothing. 2. Safety: both leave no dangling read. 3. Compile time first: both are decided when compiling, and B adds nothing at run time to any program A accepts. 4. A written word only for meaning: neither adds one, and B lets the compiler work out the fact it can see (C3). 5. The ordinary program: A makes the programmer reorder lines to suit a placement they never wrote; B changes nothing. 6. Consistency: B keeps RC-1's "a local ... becomes one of the owners", RC-7 and verdict 23, BCK-4 and VII.1's terms (none lists sharing) and verdict 103's reason (no layout outside the function changes).

decisions.title: `thread_shared` before a local stays refused, as the rule on threads says (J4-05)
decisions.problem: RC-1's sentence lists `thread_shared x` before a local. THR-1 and OWN-13 refuse it (E7017), with a message written for exactly that case, and THR-17's E7004 help and RC-7's E7014 help also say "create it shared" and "fill ... where the object is made". RC-1's sentence came from Hardened_2's write-up of verdict 103, which speaks only of `shares`. E7017 came from the redesign's rule R3 (run 4), not from an owner verdict.

options.outcome: Compiles and prints 8080. After line 10, `s.port = 9` is E7014, so `s` no longer keeps what it could do. A class object made elsewhere (a call's result, an `owns` parameter) carries the one-thread header of 8 or 12 bytes (OBJ-1) and must move to a 32-byte block at the line, which ends every view and link of it. A class object made in this function could get the 32-byte header from the start, but its fields would then sit at offset 32, not 8 or 12 (the header tables, p08 37-61), so every function it is lent to before the line would need to be compiled again for that layout. Allowing it for struct values only would make the rule differ by type.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: A costs nothing and stays safe; B needs, for class objects, either a move at run time (an allocation and a copy, cutting views and links) or a second compiled copy of every function the object is lent to before the line. 2. Safety: both are safe. 3. Compile time first: A is decided when compiling; B's move runs while the program runs. 4. A written word only for meaning: neither adds one. 5. The ordinary program: A's way is one line, `cfg = thread_shared Config(port=port)`, the same line E7014 already asks for whenever a value is changed after it is shared. 6. Consistency: A keeps THR-1, OWN-13 and the E7004 and E7014 helps, OBJ-1 (a header fixed where the value is made), verdict 101, and verdict 23 true for every local that is shared. B would make verdict 23 untrue for one word, and B for struct values only would be one rule by type (principle 4).

holes.today: Refused. `param: *mut void` on a `safe fn` is E5002 (p16-ffi.md 82-84). The only spelling the rules give for the callback is its C carrier, `cb: extern "C" fn(u32, *mut void)`, and that spelling itself says where C passes the user data.
holes.with_edit: The Ember-level checks pass: `param` is a witness (FFI-10 add), and `owns cb: thread_shared fn(u32)` is 'the C callback's [parameters], less the callback parameter that receives the user data' (FFI-21 as edited, 404-412; FFI-22 439-440). But this declaration is word for word the edit's sibling 1, whose C callback is `void(*)(void*, uint32_t)`. Here C calls `cb(elapsed_ms, param)`. Nothing written in `add_timer` decides between the two. FFI-21 417-420 ('without `@N`, exactly one parameter has that type', '1-based, as in the C signature') has no C signature to read. Read against the Ember type, it finds no parameter of `*mut void` in `fn(u32)`, or in the edit's own `owns cb: fn()`, so it makes every hand-declared callback with user data E5002.
holes.what_goes_wrong: An ordinary declaration of a timer, input or audio callback with any parameter of its own gets a C ABI that no written word fixes. Whichever position the compiler assumes, one of the two orders is wrong. With the wrong one, the trampoline reads `elapsed_ms` (16) as the tagged number, and FFI-53's check stops the program at the first tick with the misleading 'C called the callback ... after its token ended'. The callback's `elapsed_ms` would receive the user-data bits. Under the literal reading of 417-420, the edit's own FFI-52 example and all three siblings' hand declarations are E5002. Either way FFI-10's 'the compiler checks that mapping and lowers it to the C ABI carrier' is no longer decided by the declaration. The check that `remove_timer`'s `cb: extern "C" fn(u32, *mut void)` matches the registering call's carrier (FFI-11 303-304) has nothing to compare against. The timer is a real C++-style danger: a trampoline that treats the wrong argument register as its user-data pointer.
holes.rule_lines: p16-ffi.md 404-412 as edited ('a function value whose parameters and result are the C callback's, less the callback parameter that receives the user data'); 417-420 (`user_data=p@N`, 'as in the C signature', 'exactly one parameter has that type, or the contract is E5002'); 79-82 (FFI-10: a safe fn writes the Ember types and 'the compiler checks that mapping and lowers it to the C ABI carrier'); 493 as edited (FFI-52's `owns cb: fn()`); FFI-53 515-523 (the tagged-number check).
holes.fix_hint: Keep the written declaration the whole C ABI: the user data's place among the C callback's parameters is said by `user_data=p@N`, counted in the C callback, and required whenever the Ember function type has parameters of its own (the 'exactly one parameter has that type' test then reads that C callback).

holes.today: FFI-21 404-405 already gives C 'the block's tagged number as the user data', whatever the user data's C type. A 64-bit tagged number goes into a 32-bit `int`, and no rule refuses it.

break-engineering:K31-c-kept-callback-de.notes:
Verdict: the edit holds for the cases it names, but one high hole is caused by the edit, so broken is true. The hand-over part is sound: the callback is taken `owns`, the call says `owns`, the result is the token, and `ud` is a witness. It is better grounded than the edit says: CLO-7 (p06-expressions.md 318-322) already takes a function that is kept past the call `owns` for standard-library functions; THR-17 (p11-concurrency.md 183-186) puts a kept C callback beside unscoped threads; Appendix F (p24-appx-f.md 29) calls a kept callback 'a function value C keeps after the call that hands it over'. No verdict is widened. The ordinary program costs one word, and run time does not change.

The high hole (first hole): writing the callback parameter as an Ember function type takes the C callback's signature out of the hand declaration, and nothing written puts back where the user data sits in it. `owns cb: thread_shared fn(u32)` is the same text for `void(*)(void*, uint32_t)` (the edit's sibling 1, where the answer reads the order from a comment) and for `void(*)(uint32_t, void*)` (SDL_AddTimer's order; glibc's and BSD's `qsort_r` differ in exactly this). FFI-21 417-420 ('as in the C signature', 'exactly one parameter has that type') has no C signature to read. Read against the Ember type, it makes every hand-declared user-data callback E5002, the edit's own FFI-52 example included. The repair is a property: the declaration fixes the whole C ABI. Overlays are unaffected, because the header supplies the C signature.

Low, caused by the edit: FFI-22's E7015 message (p16-ffi.md 450) still gives `register_cb(fn() thread_shared game: ...)`, which is now E3028. The edit flags this and leaves it to the lead.

Pre-existing, for the gap list (not holes of this edit):
- The user-data witness's C type: an `int` cookie truncates the 64-bit tagged number. The edit's to_verify claim 'ud: i32 is E5002' has no words behind it.
- The call word for a borrowed callback (the edit's gap 2).
- How destroys(f)'s parameters match the registering call's (FFI-11 303-304). By name, sibling 1's `timer_cancel(cb, ud)` does not match `timer_start(..., on_tick, ud)`, so 'timer's end cancels the timer' rests on an unstated match.
- Two callbacks of one registering call that share one user-data parameter: FFI-21's 'a block of its own' gives two tagged numbers for one slot.
- Whether `callback(once)` takes a `once fn` (left to K53). Under the edit's words, a once callback written `owns cb: fn()` would refuse a lambda that hands a capture on (E3013, CLO-6).

Edit mechanics: the FFI-10 'add' is assumed to be inserted after the quoted sentence (lines 91-92), not to replace it. Even if it replaced it, lines 109-110 keep the unsafe raw declaration's written parameters.

Nothing was run. Every must_run expectation assumes the C stub described in the test.

holes.what_goes_wrong: A correct one-thread program is refused (a compiler front end's diagnostic linked to its source file, a UI error linked to its widget), with no safety gained: it never erases the error and never touches a thread. The owner_short line 'as Rust's anyhow requires' describes A's shape (Rust's Error trait has no Send parent; anyhow asks Send + Sync at its conversion). break-engineering:K20-anyerror-send.notes:
Engineering lens. Nothing was run. Every program was walked against the part files.

The edit answers its own question: J6-16 compiles at no run-time cost, and the routes (a thread's result, a channel, a lock scoped tasks share, a thread_shared holder) follow from THR-8's existing words for `dyn` and `owns`.

It is broken by three medium holes caused by the edit:
(1) Requiring Send and ThreadShared of every error type refuses correct one-thread programs that never erase an error. The decision's two reasons for preferring C over A are wrong: the language already has a type for an erased value that may cross threads (`dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, p03-grammar.md 72 and 171; decisions.md 141), so A needs no hidden special path; and A does not refuse at least as many programs (hole 1's program). Owner_short's 'as Rust's anyhow requires' describes A's shape: Rust's Error trait has no Send parent, and anyhow asks Send + Sync at its From conversion. A does make ERR-1 p13 46-47 untrue, and ERR-1 is outside the allowed rules, so the repair may have to end as owner_question with both reaches stated correctly.
(2) ThreadShared cannot be vouched (TYP-43 p04 592-594), so an error type holding a raw pointer or a foreign handle can no longer be an Error at all.
(3) The stated fix for a `shares` field (`thread_shared`) runs into E7014 for any linked value the program changes (THR-1 p11 77-81). Its real cost is a lock per access, not 'nothing on one thread', and it clashes with verdict 73.

Low holes: the generic error type's instances are left undecided (to_verify assumes per instance); ERR-3's prose ('kept to one thread') is narrower than its needs list (Cell, `ref mut`, plain `fn()`); IV.8's definitions (p04 600-601, 676) contradict the edited ERR-3 until they change.

Pre-existing, for the gap list: THR-2's hand-over check (verdict 114 fix 1) does not say how it reaches an object of a weakref'd class owned inside an erased value, or what that costs. The edit makes every AnyError such a value, and its 'no instruction is added on any path' leaves this out.

Evidence problems in the answer, not holes of the rule:
- Sibling 2 as written is E3013 at `g.push(owns e)`, because `match r:` binds a view (OWN-10 p07 113-115). It needs `match owns r:`.
- Sibling 1's `match page_size(path):` on a call result is not plainly a place the match takes over. The test uses `r = ...` then `match owns r:`.
- Sibling 4's 'today: compiles' needs a Debug for a weakref field, which the TYP-36 table (p04 703-718) does not give.

Two further programs found nothing new: a BatchError holding Array[AnyError] returned from a worker, and a generic `[E: needs Error]` function spawning with `owns e`. Every std error type passes the new needs (read from std/src).

checked: J6-16, line by line. Today: refused at the spawn line, E7015. The result must be Send (p11 175-176). AnyError holds `owns dyn Error` (p13 93-94). `owns T` is Send only when T is (p11 48), and `dyn I` only when I requires it (p11 51); Error requires only Debug and Display (p13 87-88, p04 676). With the edit: the new p13 88 makes `dyn Error` Send by p11 51, and ThreadShared by p11 60 ('inferred like Send'). So `Result[int, AnyError]` is Send, and the spawn compiles. `h.join()?` hands the AnyError on with no call (p13 51-54). A missing file prints `error: <message>` on stderr and exits 1 (p13 109-112). The stated outcome is CONFIRMED.

Sibling 1 (a channel of AnyError). CONFIRMED: today it compiles by THR-15 (p11 336-337, Sender is Send whatever it carries), refused under lead fix J7-07, and compiles with the edit. Spelling note: `match page_size(path):` is safer written `match owns page_size(path):` before `owns e` (p03 507-513).

Sibling 2 (`Mutex[Array[AnyError]]` shared by scoped tasks). The thread outcome is CONFIRMED: Mutex is ThreadShared for a Send T (p11 66). But the program as written is refused for an unrelated reason. `match r:` binds `e` as a read-only view (p03 507-509), so `g.push(owns e)` hands over a view. It needs `match owns r:` (p03 512-513).
Sibling 3 (`shares SourceFile` in a ParseError). CONFIRMED: today it compiles, and with the edit it is E2040 at the derive line. The help it gives does not compile on its own: hole 6.
Sibling 4 (`weakref Widget` in a LayoutError). CONFIRMED: E2040 with the edit, compiles today. The same refusal falls on a one-thread program that never makes an AnyError: hole 1.

verdicts_kept: 3, 23, 61, 94, 101, 104, 110, 114, 151, 164, 165 and 166 are not reversed or widened by the edited words. Verdict 164's and verdict 166's texts are not yet in THR-8 or THR-11 (p11 43-58, p11 405-406), so safety on those routes waits for those verdicts to land. That gap was already there.
THR-9's 'inferred like Send' (p11 60), read for `dyn I` and `owns T`: it gives `dyn Error` and AnyError ThreadShared. Still to confirm on the compiler.
TYP-43 (p04 592-593): ThreadShared cannot be vouched for by hand, so no `unsafe extend ... implements Send` type can be an error (hole 3).
LT-45, TYP-15, LT-1 and LT-22 for errors that hold views, once erased into AnyError (pre-existing gap PE1).
THR-2's hand-over walk (verdict 114) for weakref'd objects inside an erased value (pre-existing gap PE2).
Verdict 166, for a scoped task that ends an AnyError whose error owns an object a link points at (test T14).
Class families: a subclass of an error class that holds a `shares` field (test T15). Decided by the edit's 'every error type' words.
Generic error types (hole 2), errors holding a Cell (hole 4), raw-pointer errors (hole 3), and p04 459/676 against the edited ERR-3 (hole 5).
Two programs in a row found nothing new: jobs.submit with an AnyError capture (T9) and two scoped tasks reading one AnyError (T8).

A view inside an error keeps the value from outliving what it views (LT-45 p07 654-659, TYP-15 p04 311-317), and no such value reaches an unscoped thread (THR-2 p11 105-106). Handing an object over moves its weakref'd contents (THR-2 p11 112-122). Gaps PE1 (a region through erasure) and PE2 (the walk inside an erased value) were already there.

holes.with_edit: The same. The routes the edit opens (a thread's result, a channel, `owns e` into thread.spawn) add places where THR-8's 'a Send view never goes to an unscoped thread' (p11 52-53) is judged by AnyError's type, which shows no view.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A view hidden in an erased value can outlive its source, on one thread today and across threads with the edit, unless region tracking through `owns dyn I` and through non-view call results is stated.
holes.fix_hint: A value that may hold a view keeps that view's region through erasure and through every call result, whatever its declared type.

holes.program:
import std.thread

class Widget:
    label: String

interface Job: needs Send:
    fn run()

struct Repaint implements Job:
    target: Widget

    fn run():
        println(f"repainting {this.target.label}")

fn main():
    confirm = Widget(label=String("Confirm purchase"))
    link = weakref confirm
    job: owns dyn Job = owns Repaint(target=owns confirm)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns job: job.run())
    if link exists as w:
        println(w.label)
    h.join()
holes.today: THR-2's words (p11 119-122) move every object the handed object owns 'whose class a weakref is made to anywhere in the program (the compiler knows those classes; one compare each)'. So `confirm` should move, `link` should find it ended, and the program prints `repainting Confirm purchase`. But inside `owns dyn Job` the kind is known only while running. No rule gives the hand-over a way into an erased value (TYP-22 p04 792-795 gives Clone a method-table entry; nothing gives this one), and no cost is stated. If the walk misses it, main opens `link` while the worker uses or ends the widget: a race on its header, and a read of freed memory.
holes.with_edit: The same mechanism, now reached by every AnyError handed over: an error that owns a weakref'd class object (`Detached(name: String, widget: Widget)`) inside an AnyError captured with `owns e` (test T13).
holes.what_goes_wrong: Verdict 114's safety on erased values rests on a mechanism the text does not give. The edit's 'cost: none' leaves out that AnyError hand-overs now run that walk.
holes.rule_lines: p11-concurrency.md 112-122; p04-types.md 785-795
holes.fix_hint: An erased value's method table lets a hand-over reach every object it owns, and the cost (one indirect call per erased value, plus one compare per object) is stated.

break-safety:K20-anyerror-send.notes:
The safety core holds. Every Error implementer must be Send and ThreadShared, so `dyn Error` and AnyError get both markers from THR-8's existing rule for erased values (p11 48, 51) and from THR-9's 'inferred like Send' (p11 60). Errors that hold a `shares` owner, a weakref link to a one-thread value, a Cell or a raw pointer are refused. No vouched type can be an error, because ThreadShared cannot be vouched for (TYP-43). I found no program the edited words let through that races, double-ends or has undefined behaviour beyond gaps that were already there.

Why broken is true: hole 1 (medium, a correct program refused). Under C, a one-thread error type holding a link or a `shares` owner is refused even when it never becomes an AnyError and never leaves its thread. Under A, and today, it compiles. The decision's step 6 claim that A has 'the same practical reach' is untrue for every program that keeps a concrete error type (ERR-9). The owner should see that before reviewing C. The other holes the edit causes are low: generic error types (where the refusal lands), raw-pointer errors (never errors at all), prose that misnames the property (a Cell is not 'kept to one thread'; a view-holding error does not 'go to another thread' freely), p04 676 and 459 still showing the old parents (they must land together), and sibling 3's one-line help, which does not compile on its own.

Gaps that were already there, for the list (not holes of this edit):
- PE1: a view inside an erased error. LT-22's call-result summaries reach only view and view-type results, so AnyError can carry a dangling view on one thread today. The edit's thread routes widen the reach.
- PE2: THR-2's verdict-114 walk inside an erased value has no stated mechanism or cost. It applies to every `dyn I: needs Send` today and to every AnyError with the edit.
- Safety on two routes depends on answered verdicts whose text has not landed: verdict 164 (sharedref mut is not Send, still missing from THR-8 p11 43-58) and verdict 166 (a task ending a linked object, missing from THR-11 p11 405-406). Test T14 checks the second.
- A one-thread memory manager (`owns T using A`) inside an error freed on another thread is P02/J5-05, unchanged by this edit.

Program-text defects in the answer, not caused by the edit:
- Sibling 2's `match r:` binds `e` as a view (p03 507-509), so `g.push(owns e)` is refused for that reason. It must be `match owns r:`.
- Sibling 1's `match page_size(path):` is safer written `match owns page_size(path):`.
- Sibling 3's `file=src` likely needs `owns src`.

Nothing was run. The expected outcomes in the tests are by the rules as written; spellings I was unsure of (a subclass constructor, `struct ... implements Job:` with a method body, `Cell` from the prelude) are for the lead to fix before the tests run on the compiler.

break-engineering:K06-sharing-a-local.notes:
I read the edit only; nothing was run. Every program in the answers and siblings does what the edit says under the edited words: J5-06 prints 5, 6; J4-05 is E7017 at line 10; the help lines compile; Viewport, Interner, Team, FrameStats and Log behave as stated; Dispatcher is E3021 at line 13. I set broken to true because of one medium hole that the edit causes.

Hole 1 is in the added HEAP-3 sentence. It uses VII.1's 'into X' (p07 34-36), which goes all the way down, so a StrView or a span into a buffer the local owns also forces the earlier block. Sharing moves only the local's own bytes. That buffer never moves, so safety needs nothing there. The result is an allocation and a free per round on the path that does not share. The edit's own Interner sibling is an example; in a parser loop the cost is per line. The repair is a property: only what points at the local's own bytes (a field view, a position, a captured `ref`, a link) needs the earlier block.

Holes 2 and 3 are low and also caused by the edit. Hole 2: the COST row p10 328 still promises that nothing is allocated where no line says so. Hole 3: the wording says 'moves nothing that points into it' and 'used across' instead of BCK-2's 'live'.

Holes 4 to 6 were there before the edit:
- Whether `thread_shared` may come before a call's result (a factory or loader, or `copy of` with a user `clone()`). The edit's why_general claims 'a call's result' is refused, but neither its words nor BRW-12's 'new value' say so.
- What `=` on a local means after it is shared. In an ordinary batching loop the two readings print different output.
- Whether a view of a list local made before the sharing line stays a position. With the edit both readings are safe, but which one holds is still unsaid.

On J4-05's decision, reason (b) is the weakest of the three. Any function a `thread_shared` object of that class is lent to already needs the 32-byte layout (decisions.md section 2's twin type index), so the claimed second compiled copy is mostly already paid. Reasons (a) and (c) carry option A on their own: an object made elsewhere would have to move, and under B verdict 23's 'keeps what it could do' would stop being true for `thread_shared`. A stands. The readability cost is real for a configuration filled field by field in a loop. E7017's help must still compile there: fold the filling lines into the making line, as E7014's help does.

Process points for the lead, outside my lens:
- The outcome is labelled `decided`, yet both entries in `decisions` were chosen by parameters. J5-06 option B adds a run-time cost on paths that do not share. J4-05 option A changes what RC-1 says, and E7017 rests on rule R3, not on a verdict (owner_short says so).

Left to the safety lens:
- A raw pointer from `ref_to_ptr` is not a view, so the words do not cover it, although the edit's notes say they do.
- Whether `shares mut inv` while a `ref mut` view of `inv.gold` is live is E3021 under BRW-1. It is safe either way under the edit.

A cheaper mechanism worth measuring: compile the views of a local that does not escape against the local's current address, which the sharing line updates. That needs no allocation on the fast path. Kept views and captures would still need the earlier block.

Sibling net send: CONFIRMED. The calls are told apart by count. `Socket&` imports as `ref mut socket: Socket`, so the call writes `ref mut sock` (FFI-40, p21 161-162; FN-2a, p05 115-127).

Sibling queue: REFUTED AS WRITTEN. `q = eng.jobs.Queue.new()` sits outside `unsafe:`, and there is no overlay. A header function with no entry 'stays unsafe to call' (FFI-2, p16 40-41), so the line is E3100 (code table, p17a-codes.md 164). Moved inside `unsafe:`, the program is CONFIRMED: `push(first)` fits only the plain `push(const Job&)`; `push(owns second)` fits only `push(Job&&)`, imported as `owns job: Job` (verdicts 146, 147); a later `second.id` is E3040 (verdict 145, p17a 141).

Sibling mixer overlay: REFUTED AS WRITTEN, for three reasons. main.em uses `c_int` without `from std.ffi import c_int` (`std.ffi` holds the C aliases, p15-stdlib.md 71). The two `set_volume` entries are E5010 by FFI-30c (H1). And `level: f32` is a contract word by GRM-35's 'Contract words take the place of types' (p16 277), against the new FFI-12 sentence (H2). The parts that hold: the untyped `fn set_volume(level)` fits both declarations and is E5010, and a later header overload that an entry then fits stops the build. Both are CONFIRMED by the new FFI-12 sentence.

Sibling Linux seek: CONFIRMED. `long` imports as `c_long` (FFI-8, p16 173), a per-target alias (p15 71), which is `i64` on LP64. So both declarations fit `at: i64` exactly, and the call is E2070. On Windows, `c_long` is `i32` and the call runs `seek(long long)`.

The header classes with no data members (Renderer, Value, Queue, Mixer, File) are standard-layout and trivially copyable, so FFI-32 (p21 74-77) imports them by value. No stated outcome changes. My test headers give each class a `std::vector` member so that it imports opaque.
Cost claim: CONFIRMED. The choice is made when compiling. There is one thunk per declaration (FFI-17, p21 10-12) and one direct call. Nothing runs while the program runs.

Verdicts 125, 131, 132 and 134, kept per declaration: CONFIRMED. Choosing ignores safety. The chosen declaration's own entry, or the lack of one, then decides `unsafe`, `@safety`, `@ffi(const)` and L3015. One entry fits one declaration, or it is E5010.
Verdicts 145, 146, 147 at an overloaded call: CONFIRMED. The words at the call are part of fitting, so `owns` picks `T&&` and ends the name once.
`super.init(...)` with overloaded C++ base constructors: CONFIRMED. The general sentence picks what FFI-39b's first sentence picks.
Receiver-const pairs (`data()` and `data() const`, `at(i)` and `at(i) const`, left to K47): under these words they are E2070 at every call. That is a refusal, not a safety break.

My own programs: value-dependent choice (H6); typed entry fitting no declaration (H3); entry types longer than one word (H2); override of an overloaded virtual (H4); an overloaded name used as a value (H5); a function declared, then defined (H7); a `= delete` overload (H8); constructor words (H9).

A `set_limit(std::optional<int>)` and `set_limit(long long)` pair: an `i32` argument reaches both only through coercions (TYP-5 rules 11 and 1), so it is E2070; an `i64` argument fits `long long` exactly.

break-safety:K21-cpp-overloads.notes:
Process: I only read files. I used Read and Grep, and one `sed -n` to print two long lines of decisions.md (329 and 347). Nothing was run, written or changed.

Safety verdict: no program the edit admits reads freed memory, races, or ends a value twice. The `owns` and `ref mut` words at the call take part in choosing, so the chosen declaration's word governs the hand-over (verdicts 145-147). Choosing ignores safety, so an overload with no entry stays unsafe even when a sibling overload has one (verdict 125). Two overloads that are one Ember type on a target are E2070.

Why broken is true: three medium holes are caused by this edit.
- H1: FFI-30c and GRM-35 key entries and `override` by name, so the question's own overlay is also E5010.
- H2: the typed entry parameter the FFI-12 sentence needs has no grammar beyond one word, and it contradicts GRM-35 line 277 ('Contract words take the place of types'). GRM-35 is an allowed rule, so both H1 and H2 can be fixed there.
- H4: overriding one of several same-named C++ virtuals is undecided. CLS-4's by-name rule could route a `Light` call into a `Mesh` body (type confusion). This is the one hole with a path to undefined behaviour, but only under one reading.

Low holes: H3 (a typed entry that fits no declaration is not refused by the rule text), H5 (an overloaded name used as a value), H6 (TYP-5 rule 12 makes the choice depend on a known value), H7 ('declarations' read as C++ redeclarations), H8 (`= delete` overloads), H9 (FN-2a's 'a constructor's argument takes no word' against call words at `X.new`).

Corrections to the answer's evidence:
- The queue sibling calls `Queue.new()` outside `unsafe:` with no overlay, which is E3100.
- The mixer sibling's main.em lacks `from std.ffi import c_int`. An overlay has no import line, so whether `c_int` is a name inside one is not said.
- The J8-04 overlay variant's import line lacks `overlay=`.
- A class with no data members imports by value (FFI-32).
- FFI-2 (p16 40-42) names E5002 for a call of a function with no entry, while the code table (p17a 164) says E3100. I used E3100.

Left as the answer says: receiver-const pairs (K47) become E2070 at every call (`data()`, `at()`, `begin()`), which is a refusal. One cost note for the engineering lens: for a temporary argument (`q.push(make_job())`) Ember picks the `const T&` overload and copies, where C++ moves, unless the call writes `owns`.

checked: J8-01's program today: line 14 is E5002 (p16-ffi.md 82-84, raw `ud` on a `safe fn`), and the declaration writes no Ember type for `cb` (79-81). Confirmed.

J8-01's program with the edit: `ud` becomes a witness, so line 14's E5002 now names `cb` (C carrier instead of the produced `owns cb: fn()`) and the missing result (84: 'a type/contract mismatch is E5002, naming the slot'). Line 18 is E3028 (FN-2a p05 115-127). Confirmed, read with the C callback as `void(*)(void*)`, the only C signature with one `*mut void` and no other parameter (see hole 1 for the literal reading of 417-420).
The edited FFI-52 example (compiles, `poll_events()` runs the kept callback, `sqrt` with `no_callbacks` runs none): confirmed under the same reading, with hole 4 (unregister's `cb` type).

The edited E7004 message line `return register_cb(owns fn() owns game: game.add_point())` compiles against the edited declaration: confirmed. Its second suggestion (`fn() weakref game`) is shown without `owns` (folded into hole 5).

Sibling 1 (threads(any) timer `fn(u32)`): the `thread_shared` type, E3028 without `owns` and too many arguments are confirmed. 'Compiles' is not confirmed: nothing in `timer_start`'s declaration says the user data is the C callback's first parameter (hole 1).

Sibling 2 (named function, threads(main)): confirmed. `owns count_frame` ends the name (FN-1 p05 88-89, E3040). Without `owns` it is E3028. FN-2a's lent sentence (p05 132-134) stays limited to the standard library.
Sibling 3 (overlay): confirmed. The header's typedef gives the C callback, so the user-data position is known. Caveat: a bare `ud` in the overlay (hole 8, pre-existing).
Verdicts 31, 39/86, 62, 91, 102, 114 fix 3, 136, 147, 150, 158, 160, 161, and FFI-22 61/94: none reversed or widened from the safety side.

CLO-4 (p06 289-300), CLO-6 (306-313), CLO-7 (318-326), CLO-16, CLO-18 against an `owns` function value given to C: a function that uses a real variable is E7004 (CLO-4 checks it against the C function's 'keeps it' summary), and a `once fn` is E3013.
FFI-53's checks and stop texts (p16 515-540): a call after the token ends, a second `once` call, and a wrong thread are all stopped before the callback's state is read.
`callback(borrowed)` under the new type words: the parameter has no word, so `owns` there is E5002. The 'moved into a block ... freed' sentence remains (hole 7, pre-existing).
Nullable kept callback `owns cb: Option[fn()]` with `register_cb(owns None)`: verdict 147 spelling, NULL and no user data (420-421). Nothing new for memory safety.
`callback(once)`: left to K53 as the edit says. A `once fn` given to `owns cb: fn()` is E3013, which is safe.
Two callbacks naming one `user_data` (hole 3).
User data not first in the C callback (hole 1).
Raw pointers in the C callback's parameters (safe: dereferencing needs unsafe) and in its result (hole 2).
A user-data slot narrower than the tagged number (hole 6).
A registering C function with a result of its own, and `destroys(f)` taking that result (hole 9).
`destroys(f)`'s parameter types against the edited `owns cb: fn()` (hole 4).
The knock-on in FFI-22's E7015 message line (p16 450) (hole 5).

Last two probes, nothing new. (a) `register_cb(owns this.on_tick)`, a function value from a field: OWN-11's partial hand-over applies and a later use is E3040. (b) A kept callback that calls `poll_events()` inside its own walk of a list it changes: E3020 by FFI-52 458-461.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed memory: what C keeps lives as long as C may call it, and nothing it uses ends first
matrix.how_kept: Kept for the function's state. The edited FFI-21 makes a kept-callback parameter `owns`, so the function value moves into the block and the caller's name ends (FN-1 p05 88-89, E3040). Only the token's end frees the block, after `destroys(f)` (FFI-23 p16 541-544), and FFI-53 534-538 makes a callback that ends its own token wait until it returns. A function that uses a real variable with no word is E7004 (FFI-21 410, CLO-7 p06 325-326), even when it comes from a variable, because CLO-4 (p06 290-295) checks it against what the C function does with it, and C keeps it. Not kept: a raw-pointer result C reads after the callback returns (hole 2).

matrix.guarantee: No data race: a callback C may run on another thread holds only what several threads may use
matrix.how_kept: Kept, and unchanged by the edit. FFI-22 (p16 438-443) makes a callback with `threads(any)`, the default, a `thread_shared fn(...)`. The edited declaration writes that type, and FFI-10 84's mapping check refuses a plain `fn()` there (E5002, 'a type/contract mismatch'). A `shares mut` capture is E7015. FFI-53 checks `creator` and `main` callbacks on every call.

from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Game:
    score: i32 = 0

    fn add_point():
        this.score += 1

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `audio_watch` was given")
    unsafe fn audio_unwatch(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    # audio.c: audio_pump() starts the mixing thread, which calls cb(ud) once, and joins it
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(any)), destroys(audio_unwatch))
    safe fn audio_watch(owns cb: thread_shared fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn audio_pump()

fn main():
    game = shares mut Game()
    w = audio_watch(owns fn() shares mut game: game.add_point())
    audio_pump()
    println(game.score)

from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Hud:
    elapsed_total: u32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`tick` and `ud` are a pair `clock_subscribe` was given")
    unsafe fn clock_unsubscribe(tick: extern "C" fn(u32, *mut void), ud: *mut void)
    # clock.h: typedef void (*clock_tick)(uint32_t elapsed_ms, void *ud);  the user data is the LAST parameter
    @ffi(param(tick, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(clock_unsubscribe))
    safe fn clock_subscribe(owns tick: fn(u32), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn clock_advance(ms: u32)

fn main():
    hud = shares mut Hud()
    sub = clock_subscribe(owns fn(ms: u32) shares mut hud: hud.elapsed_total += ms)
    clock_advance(16)
    println(hud.elapsed_total)
holes.today: Refused. `ud: *mut void` is a raw-pointer parameter on a `safe fn`, which is E5002 (p16-ffi.md 82-84), and no rule gives `tick` an Ember type.
holes.with_edit: `ud` becomes a witness (edited FFI-10). `tick`'s type is the C callback's parameters 'less the callback parameter that receives the user data' (edited FFI-21). But the declaration no longer writes the C callback, so nothing says the user data is its second parameter. FFI-21 417-420 finds that parameter either by `@N`, counted 'as in the C signature', or as the only parameter of the user data's type, and gives E5002 otherwise. Read against the written `fn(u32)`, no parameter has that type, so this program, the edit's own FFI-52 example (`fn()`) and siblings 1 and 2 are all E5002. Read against the C signature, there is no C signature written. A compiler that builds the trampoline as `void(void*, uint32_t)` (sibling 1's order) reads 16 as the tagged number, and the program stops at `clock_advance(16)` with 'C called the callback registered on line 16 after its token ended; it was unregistered'.
holes.what_goes_wrong: An ordinary callback that takes an argument of its own (a timer's elapsed time, a key code, a log level) gets no stated C ABI from a hand declaration. Under one reading the question's own program is refused. Under the other, the program stops on the first call with a message that blames the token. On a 32-bit target the tagged number may be a user-space address (FFI-53 519-520), so the check that would catch a misread argument is weaker there. In C++ terms: calling a function through a pointer cast to the wrong signature.
holes.rule_lines: p16-ffi.md 400-405 and 417-420 (FFI-21 as edited); 79-82 (FFI-10: the compiler 'lowers it to the C ABI carrier'); 515-521 (FFI-53); the edited FFI-52 line `safe fn register_cb(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void)`
holes.fix_hint: Every C ABI fact the trampoline needs, including where the user data sits among the C callback's parameters, comes from a written word (the header, or the C callback signature in the hand declaration), and the Ember type is derived from it, never the reverse.

holes.today: Refused. `ud: *mut void` on a `safe fn` is E5002 (p16-ffi.md 82-84), and no rule gives `title` an Ember type.
holes.with_edit: Compiles. The edited FFI-21 makes `title`'s Ember type 'a function value whose parameters and result are the C callback's', so the result is `const char*`, which FFI-8 (p16 180) maps to `*c_char`. FFI-10 82-84 refuses only a raw-pointer parameter or result of the `safe fn` itself, and the edit's new FFI-10 sentence exempts `ud`. `ref_to_ptr` is safe (p04-types.md 340-342). FFI-21a's E5042 (p16 424-434) covers only a pointer into a by-value parameter copy of an `extern "C" fn`. So `ui_run_frame()` makes C copy from `frame_title`'s stack frame after it has returned, and the program has no `unsafe` line.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A safe program makes C read freed memory, which in C++ terms is returning a pointer to a local array. ODR-073 says a `safe fn` 'exposes the mapped safe Ember type, never a raw pointer' (p26 361). The callback's result is a raw pointer that safe code fills and C trusts. (One could read FFI-1's per-pointer facts, p16 26-28, as reaching the callback's own pointer result and refusing this program. The edited words do not say so, and they state the C type as the Ember type.)
holes.rule_lines: p16-ffi.md 400-405 (FFI-21 as edited); 82-84 (FFI-10); 180 and 188 (FFI-8); 424-434 (FFI-21a); 596-598 (FFI-56: a safe C function pointer needs scalar or `@layout(c)` parameters and result); p04-types.md 340-342 (ref_to_ptr is safe)
holes.fix_hint: The callback's own parameters and result are mapped by the same rule as the declaration's own slots: on a `safe fn`, a raw pointer among them is E5002, as FFI-56 already requires of a safe C function pointer, until a contract word maps it.

from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained, c_int

class Hud:
    ticks: int = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    # timer.c: int timer_add(void (*cb)(void *ud), void *ud) returns an id; void timer_remove(int id); void timer_fire_all(void)
    safe fn timer_remove(id: c_int)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(timer_remove))
    safe fn timer_add(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn timer_fire_all()

fn watch_once(owns hud: shares mut Hud):
    t = timer_add(owns fn() owns hud: hud.ticks += 1)
    timer_fire_all()

fn main():
    hud = shares mut Hud()
    watch_once(shares mut hud)
    timer_fire_all()
    println(hud.ticks)

holes.with_edit: Compiles. FFI-10 79-81 with FFI-21 415 (as the edited FFI-52 example shows) puts the token in the result slot, so C's `int` result has no written place. FFI-11 303-304 says `destroys(timer_remove)` takes 'the registering call's ... result', which 'the token keeps', but nothing says what C type the token reads from the call. If the call is lowered as returning nothing, the token keeps no id. `timer_remove(<anything>)` then removes another live timer, or none. In the second case C still calls the freed slot, and the second `timer_fire_all()` stops with 'C called the callback registered on line 14 after its token ended; it was unregistered', although C was never told. A C result returned through a hidden pointer (a struct of three `uint64_t`) would be written through the first argument register.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The common 'register returns an id, unregister takes it' C API (timers, signal handlers, event buses) has no stated ABI in a hand declaration. The outcomes range from removing the wrong timer, to a stop with a false message, to a memory write through a wrong pointer (C++: calling a function returning a struct by value as if it returned void).

holes.fix_hint: Same property as hole 1: a hand declaration writes every C ABI fact, including the registering function's own C result, and the token keeps it as that written type. A registering function whose C result has no place is E5002.

break-safety:K06-sharing-a-local.notes:
Safety lens; nothing was run. AUTOPILOT.md and HANDOFF.md were skipped, as the task says. I read RULES-FOR-EVERY-AGENT.md, owner-bar.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, the verdicts in the input (23, 81, 101, 103, 114, 165, with JOB.md 180-219) and decisions.md sections 1-6.

Every program in the answer checks out under the rules with the edit: J5-06, J4-05, all six siblings and the readability example give the stated outcomes and line numbers. The RC-1 change (J4-05) opens nothing. `thread_shared` stays limited to values made that way, which keeps OBJ-1's header fixed where a value is made. E7017 is the only code, except for one-owner parts, where E2122 also fits (pre-existing; the lead's to settle).

`broken` is true because of three medium holes in the HEAP-3 sentence's mechanism. Its first clause ('moves nothing that points into it') is general, but the condition and placement that follow are narrower:
- Hole 1: the condition is per line. A view made and used inside the sharing line (a plain argument next to `shares mut inv` in one call) is not 'used across the line'.
- Hole 2: the block is placed 'where the local begins', but the sharing line may name an arena that does not exist there yet (ALC-1). A text-view program that compiles safely today becomes undecided, and its inline-field sibling has no safe outcome.
- Hole 3: the placement is per local, not per value. A local given a new value after it is shared and then shared again is left with no block for the new value, or with a reading that overwrites another owner's value.

On rule F: strictly, holes 1 and 3 also dangle without the edit. I filed them against the edit because the edit claims the property for 'every kind of pointer into a local' and 'every path', and its words do not reach these members of its own class. The lead may reclassify them as pre-existing; hole 2 is a regression either way.

One property repair covers all three without growing the text: the early block is per value and per point, only for what points into the local's own storage, from the memory the sharing names. Where that memory does not exist yet, the crossing view is E3060. The same narrowing also removes hole 5's hidden allocation in the Interner sibling, whose view is into heap text that never moves.

Pre-existing gaps for the list:
- Hole 4, high: handing a shared struct local over into an inline one-owner place is undecided, and could be a silent copy or a double free.
- Hole 6, low: what 'a new value' means before `thread_shared` (a call's result).
- Unclear: whether making an owner while a `ref mut` view of the local is live counts as a read (see test ref_mut_across_sharing_read_through_owner).

Four further programs found nothing new: a position surviving a push through the other owner, a local shared every round of a loop, a scoped task reading across the sharing, and the E7007/E7015/E3040/E3060 refusals. The stop condition holds.

Fixed J8-08 program: `@safety` above `unsafe fn` (verdicts 120, 133). The wrapper's `ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8]` follows p07-ownership.md 820-825. `as_mut_ptr()` is safe to take (SPN-8, p07 837-838). `clear(ref mut frame)` converts the Array (SPN-1, p07 812-814). It compiles. Confirmed.
Sibling readv: `Span[IoVec]` with `count(iovcnt)`. Today accepted. After the edit, E5002 for `IoVec.base` behind `iov`. Confirmed.
Sibling `@ffi(safe) type PFN_mix_block`: today accepted (p16 596-598). After the edit, E5002 under FFI-56 as edited. Calls through the type stay E3100 (593-594). Confirmed.
Sibling Token, `lex_next` result and `print_token` parameter: both E5002 under the edited words. The parameter half is confirmed and needed. The result half is refused needlessly (hole 1).
Sibling blit overlay, `borrowed one` and `borrowed one exclusive`: E5002 for `Surface.pixels` behind both. Confirmed.
