causes.cause: The no-word loan reached every parameter of a standard-library function ('whatever parameter it fills'), instead of only a parameter the function's first line declares as a function. That declaration is what 'that takes one' and ODR-240's 'callable-taking' say.

What a call keeps of a lent function was the caller's real variable, used as a lambda uses one, instead of the function the variable holds. So the variable could be given another function underneath it.

repair:K21-cpp-overloads.intent: Create a renderer with its (width, height) constructor, then draw a mesh and a sprite, each through the C++ `draw` overload that matches its type.

existing_rule.words: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`)

edits.before: except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types.
edits.after: except operator-interface implementations, `extend` blocks for different types, and the functions a C++ header declares under one name, with their overrides: the header, not the program, named them (`[FFI-39b]`).
edits.why_general: E1030 says the program gave one name to two functions. For a header's set that would be untrue (principle 6), and the exception gives the reason: the header named them. It covers every scope and kind a header declares: constructors (`new`), methods, static and free functions, and listed instantiations. It also covers an Ember class's overrides of an overloaded virtual, which take the header's name. A name the program gives stays E1030: two functions an overlay renames into one name, or an overlay `extend` method named like a header method. A header's own name renamed as a whole (`rename draw as render`) is still the header's set.

edits.before: no declared `init` is `E5058`.
edits.after: Every use of a name a header declares several functions under means the one C++ would take there, of those it fits by type, not value, and by the words at a call, each type read as the C++ type it is (`c_long` is `long`, `i64` `long long`, a literal as in C++, a type C++ lacks as the parameter's). A use none fits is `E2020`, and one C++ refuses `E2070`, naming each.
edits.why_general: One property covers every use of such a name: a call, an `override`, a function value, and `super.init` (whose arity-and-type pick is C++'s). The use means what the header's own language takes there, so the header's design decides: a literal `7` takes `int` beside `float`, a derived object the nearer base, and a deleted or ambiguous choice is refused. Ember's rules decide what may be reached: by type only, never by a known value, and only with the words a call writes (`ref mut` for `T&`, `owns` for `T&&`, verdicts 146 and 147). Each type is read as the C++ type it is, which keeps C's names apart (`c_long` is `long`, `i64` is `long long`), so every function of a set can be reached on every target. The choice is made when compiling.

edits.before: since a macro has no C declaration to read (ODR-147).
edits.after: Any entry may write a parameter whole, as the import gives it, before its contract words (`owns job: Job`, `values: *f32 borrowed count(n)`); wherever entries are counted, replaced or recorded, an entry stands for the one function its name and parameters fit, types read as in `[FFI-39b]`; none or several is `E5010`, naming each.
edits.why_general: Property: an entry stands for exactly one function, identified by what the import shows of it, wherever entries matter: a second entry (FFI-30c), `override`, and the record (FFI-55). The parameter is written in Ember's own parameter spelling (`[param_word] IDENT ":" type`). Ember's lambda parameters already take an optional type that way, and a macro_fn entry already writes one. So any type the import gives can be written: a word before the name, a pointer, a span, a container. If a header later adds a function that an entry fits, the build stops at that entry, and a slip that fits nothing is refused, so nothing is vouched for unread. Entries whose names or counts already tell the functions apart do not change.

answers.question: J8-04
answers.today: Not decided. TYP-26 (p04-types.md 867-868) makes the two `new` and the two `draw` E1030. FFI-20a (p16-ffi.md 162-164) skips them as declarations the importer cannot represent. FFI-39b (p21-annex-c.md 128-130) picks a constructor by arity and argument types, but only at `super.init`. Under FFI-30c (p16-ffi.md 221-222) the overlay's second `new` and second `draw` are each 'a second entry for one name', which is E5010. No overlay entry can name one of two functions that share count and parameter names. The C++ danger: overload resolution silently choosing another function through an implicit conversion.
answers.after: Compiles. `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` runs `Renderer(int, int)`, the only one two arguments fit. `r.draw(mesh)` runs `draw(const Mesh&)` and `r.draw(hud)` runs `draw(const Sprite&)`, the only one each argument's type reaches. With no overlay, each function called gets verdict 134's single `L3015`. With the overlay, each entry stands for the one function its count or parameter names fit, so the four entries are four functions' entries, never a second entry for one, and the calls need no `unsafe:`. A use C++ would refuse (two equal, or a deleted one chosen) is `E2070`. A use that fits none is `E2020`. Both errors name every function of the name.
answers.decides: TYP-26's exception (p04-types.md 868) lets the header's two `new` and two `draw` stand under one name. The sentence added to FFI-39b (p21-annex-c.md after 130) says which function each use means. The sentence added to GRM-35 (p16-ffi.md after 267) makes each overlay entry stand for one function wherever entries are counted, replaced or recorded.

sibling_cases.case: An audio mixer whose overloads share their parameter name, vouched by typed overlay lines, called with an integer and a float literal
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles with no `unsafe:`. `7` can become `c_int` or `f32`, so both fit, and C++ takes `set_volume(int)` for the literal `7`. `0.25` can only become a float, so `set_volume(float)` runs. Each typed entry stands for one function. Written as `fn set_volume(level)`, the entry fits both and is `E5010`, naming both. An entry written `fn set_volume(level: f64)` fits neither and is `E5010` too.

sibling_cases.case: A server's text builder with int, long, long long and double overloads, where long and long long are both 64-bit on Linux
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. `count` is an `int` (`i64`), read as `long long`, so `append(long long)` runs. `count as c_long` is read as `long`, so `append(long)` runs, although both are 64-bit here. `7` is C++'s `int`, so `append(int)` runs, and `0.5` runs `append(double)`. On Windows, where `c_long` is 32-bit, the same four lines run the same four functions. Every function of the set has a spelling that reaches it.

sibling_cases.case: A game engine's job queue with the `const T&` / `T&&` pair, told apart by the word at the call
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `1 2`. A call without a word fits only `push(const Job&)`, imported as `job: Job`, because verdict 147 asks for `owns` for the other. `owns second` fits only `push(Job&&)`, imported as `owns job: Job`, because verdict 146 refuses `owns` for a parameter that only reads. A later `println(second.id)` is `E3040` (verdict 145). An overlay would vouch for the pair with `fn push(job: Job)` and `fn push(owns job: Job)`.

sibling_cases.case: A calculator's AST visitor whose C++ base overloads a virtual per node type, overridden twice from Ember
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `5`, `6`, `2`. Each `override` means the one `visit` whose parameters are its own, as in C++, so the trampoline sends `visit(const Add&)` to the first override and `visit(const Mul&)` to the second, and never one node type to the other's body. TYP-26's exception lets both overrides stand because the header named them. A class that overrides only one leaves the other to C++.

sibling_cases.case: A renderer's easing table taking one function of an overloaded C++ name as a value
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Given where `unsafe fn(f32) -> f32` is expected, `an.anim.smooth` means `float smooth(float)`, the one that type fits, as C++ takes `&smooth` for a `float(*)(float)`. Written `pick = an.anim.smooth` with no type expected, it is `E2070` naming both, as C++ refuses `auto pick = &smooth`.

sibling_cases.case: A network writer with narrow integer overloads: the choice never depends on a number's value
sibling_cases.outcome: `E2020` at `out.put(code)`, naming both `put`: an `int` reaches neither `u16` nor `i8` by its type, and its known value does not count. `code = -1` gives the same error, so editing the number never changes which C++ function runs. `out.put(code as u16)` compiles and runs `put(std::uint16_t)`. `out.put(200)` is `E2070`: C++ reads `200` as `int`, which reaches both equally.

decisions.title: How a C++ name declared several times reaches Ember, and which function a use of it means
decisions.problem: C++ headers declare several constructors and overloaded methods and functions under one name, while Ember's own declarations have no overloading. The spec says neither what Ember names they get nor which function a call, an override or a function value means. The compiler can work the choice out from the types at the use. Only where C++ itself cannot choose, or Ember's own rules reach none of them, is a written word (`x as T`) or a refusal left.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. Speed is equal for all four: a direct thunk call chosen when compiling. Safety: D lets a number's known value decide which function runs; A, B and C never do. Readability: A reads as the header's C++. B's invented names read worst. C lengthens every import. D needs `7 as c_int` on the commonest pair. 2. Safety (C4): A reaches only what Ember's own coercions reach by type, so there is no narrowing, and it refuses whatever C++ refuses (ties, deleted functions), so nothing is picked silently. 3. Compile time (C5): all four. 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): in A the compiler works the function out. B, C and D make the programmer write names or casts that carry no meaning. 5. The ordinary program (C2): A leaves it as written. 6. Consistency (C6): FFI-39b already picks a C++ base constructor by arity and argument types, which is C++'s pick, and A carries it to every use. TYP-26's exception gives its reason (principle 6).
decisions.departs_from_verdict: No verdict covers C++ overloads, so none is departed from. A narrows §I.6's non-goal 'function overloading' to Ember's own declarations, as TYP-26's existing exceptions already do for operator-interface implementations. Recorded for the owner's later review.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | header | declares `set_volume(float)` and `set_volume(int)` | two functions, one name |
| 2 | importer | keeps the one name | `m.set_volume` |

B: one name per overload, built from its types: `m.set_volume_int(7)`

decisions.title: How an overlay entry names one of several functions that share name, count and parameter names
decisions.problem: Overlay entries are matched by name, parameter count and parameter names, and are counted and replaced by name. `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)` share all three, so no entry can say which one it vouches for. The grammar has no way to write a parameter's type, pointer or word. The compiler cannot know which function the writer meant, so only a written word or a refusal remain.

options.outcome: Each entry stands for the one function its name and parameters fit, each parameter written as the import gives it, before its contract words. A second entry, an `override` and the record all go by that function. `fn set_volume(level)` fits both and is E5010, naming both, and an entry that fits none is E5010 too. If the header later adds a function that an entry then fits, the build stops at that entry.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "mixer.hpp":
    extend Mixer:
        fn set_volume_f(level: f32):
            # SAFETY: set_volume(float) only stores the level
            unsafe:
                this.set_volume(level)
options.outcome: No entry can name either overload, so `fn set_volume(level)` is E5010 and both stay unsafe to call. Vouching needs a wrapper with an invented name.
The one entry makes both overloads safe. If the header later adds `set_volume(void* level)`, the package's own build records it, and the new overload is vouched for without anyone reading it.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once: (c) fails safety. 2. A written word only for meaning (C3): the type in (a) says which function the entry's facts are about, which is the entry's meaning. (b) forces a bookkeeping wrapper with an invented name. 5. The ordinary program (C2): (a) changes no line where count or names already tell the functions apart. 6. Consistency (C6): (a) writes a parameter in Ember's own spelling, `[param_word] IDENT ":" type`, the way a lambda's parameter takes an optional type and a macro_fn entry already writes one. Checklist 12: add the missing syntax rather than exempt the case.

repair:K21-cpp-overloads.notes:
Process: I only read and searched files with the Read and Grep tools. I ran no shell command and changed nothing. The script measures the repair's length; I aimed at about the first answer's.

Why the repair is shaped this way. The holes have two causes. First, which of a header's functions a use of their shared name means was decided only for calls, and by Ember's two-tier ranking (TYP-24), which refuses the header's commonest pairs and lets a known value decide. The repair ties every use (call, override, function value, `super.init`) to the function C++ would take there, among those Ember's own rules reach by type and by the words at the call. Second, overlay entries were written, counted and replaced by name. The repair makes an entry stand for one function wherever entries matter, written in Ember's own parameter spelling. The first answer's FFI-12 sentence is dropped: its content now sits in GRM-35, which keeps the edit to three rules.

Pre-existing, left for the list:
- S1-9: whether an imported `X.new(owns s)` takes call words. FN-2a (p05-declarations.md 131-132, verdict 159) and FFI-40/verdict 147 already disagree for a single `T&&` constructor.
- E1-7 (two Ember overrides of an overloaded virtual were E1030 anyway) is answered in passing by TYP-26's 'with their overrides'.
- E1-9: the receiver-const pair (`Node& root()` and `const Node& root() const`) is K47's (J8-05). The sentence added to FFI-39b does not say how a read-only object name counts as a C++ `const` object.

For the lead (codes and wording outside the allowed rules):
- E2070's row in the code table reads 'ambiguous interface method' and should also cover a C++ use C++ refuses.
- FFI-30c's 'second entry for one name' could read 'for one function'.
- FFI-55's example keys records by name; overloads need a key per function.
- GRM-35 line 277, 'Contract words take the place of types', now holds where no type is written, as it already did beside macro_fn entries.
- §I.6's 'function overloading' could say 'of its own'.
- FFI-48's 'rename one in the overlay' still cannot name one function, since `rename` takes a name.

Limitations stated plainly: the choice follows C++, so a use C++ calls ambiguous (`Value(3)` beside `long long` and `double`) is refused and needs `3 as i64`. A narrow-integer pair given an `int` variable needs an `as` even when its value would fit, because values never choose.

existing_rule.words: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`)

edits.before: except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types.
edits.after: except operator-interface implementations, `extend` blocks for different types, and the functions a C++ header, not the program, declares under one name (`[FFI-39b]`).
edits.why_general: E1030 refuses two functions of one name that the program declared. A C++ header's functions under one name are not the program's, so for them that refusal would say something untrue (principle 6), and the exception says so. 'Declares under one name' counts functions, not declarations: a declare-then-define pair is one function. It covers only the header's own names. These stay E1030, as for C: an overlay that `rename`s two functions to one name, an overlay `extend` method named like a header method, and every Ember declaration.

edits.before: overlay_param := IDENT [":" contract {contract}]
edits.after: overlay_param := [param_word] IDENT [":" [type] {contract}]  -- with a type, whole as imported (owns job: Job); a contract word is no type
edits.why_general: An entry's parameter may now be written the way Ember writes any parameter: its word, its name and its type, the type as the import gives it, followed by any contract words. Examples: `fn set_volume(level: f32)`, `fn push(owns job: Job)`, `fn upload(values: *f32 borrowed count(count), count)`. A parameter written with a type is written whole, so `job: Job` names the plain parameter and `owns job: Job` the one that takes the job over. `param_word` and `type` are the language's own (p03-grammar.md 75-76), and `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries already write types (GRM-35 266-267). A contract word is never read as a type, so every entry written today parses and means what it did.

edits.before: no declared `init` is `E5058`.
edits.after: Of the functions a C++ header declares under one name, a call takes, among those its words and types reach (values checked after), one taking its arguments' own types first, a literal as its default type, then as C++ overload resolution ranks them, a literal as C++ types it, an `iN`/`uN` as `intN_t`/`uintN_t`; an override or a callable value, the one whose parameter words and types it has; an entry, the one fitting what it writes. None is `E2020`, several `E2070` (`E5010` for an entry), naming each; `override` and `[FFI-30c]` match entries by function.
edits.why_general: One property for every use of a C++ name, whether it has one function or several: a call, an override, a function used as a value and an overlay entry each take the one function they fit. Which functions a call can reach is set by Ember's own rules: the count, the words at the call (verdicts 146 and 147) and TYP-5's coercions, judged by type. Values are checked after the choice, as for any call, so a known value never changes which function runs. Among the functions reached, one taking the arguments' own types comes first, as TYP-24 ranks interface instances. After that comes C++'s own ranking, the way FFI-39b already picks a base constructor and the way the header's author expects: an integer literal ranks as C++'s `int`, a nearer base beats a farther one, and a deleted function can be chosen, which is then refused (FFI-20a). Functions that import as the same Ember type are told apart by the `<cstdint>` type C++ would see. No C++ narrowing or int-to-bool conversion ever makes a function reachable. An override or a value picks by parameter words and types; a value with no expected type fits several and is E2070. FFI-30c and `override` match entries per function. Everything is chosen when compiling.

sibling_cases.case: An audio mixer's overlay for two overloads that share a parameter name, called with literals
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles with no `unsafe:`, since each entry fits one function. `m.set_volume(7)` reaches both, because an integer literal may become `c_int` or `f32`. Neither takes the literal's own type `int`, so C++'s ranking decides: `7` is an `int` there, an exact fit for `set_volume(int)`. `m.set_volume(0.25)` reaches only `set_volume(float)`. Written as `fn set_volume(level)`, the entry fits both and is `E5010`, naming both. If `mixer.hpp` later adds a third `set_volume`, an untyped entry stops the build instead of silently vouching for it.

sibling_cases.case: A scene graph's visitor whose virtual `visit` is overloaded, with one overridden from Ember
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `36`. The override has the parameter word and type of `visit(const Mesh&)`, imported as `mesh: Mesh`, so it replaces that function. The trampoline passes only that one to Ember, and `visit(const Light&)` keeps C++'s body. A `Light` never reaches a body that reads a `Mesh`. An override whose parameters fit neither is `E2020`, naming both.

readability.before:
import cpp "renderer.hpp" with (project="engine") as eng

fn main():
    mesh = eng.gfx.Mesh(vertices=36)
    hud = eng.gfx.Sprite(frame=2)
    # SAFETY: the renderer draws only what it is given, during the call
    unsafe:
        r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)
        r.draw(mesh)
        r.draw(hud)
# today: E1030, a skipped import, or a pick; the spec does not say which
# overlay lines today: fn new(width, height) / fn draw(mesh) / fn draw(sprite), the second of each name E5010, and no line can name set_volume(float level) apart from set_volume(int level)
readability.after:
import cpp "renderer.hpp" with (project="engine") as eng

fn main():
    mesh = eng.gfx.Mesh(vertices=36)
    hud = eng.gfx.Sprite(frame=2)
    # SAFETY: the renderer draws only what it is given, during the call
    unsafe:
        r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)
        r.draw(mesh)
        r.draw(hud)
# compiles: each call takes the function its arguments reach, ranked as C++ ranks them
# overlay lines: unchanged; a type only where count and names do not tell functions apart: fn set_volume(level: f32) / fn push(owns job: Job)
readability.verdict: No longer and no harder. The program's lines are unchanged and read the way the header does, with no invented names, and calls with literals (`m.set_volume(7)`) need no cast. An overlay line gains a type only where two functions share every parameter name, and only on that line, in Ember's own parameter form.

repair:K21-cpp-overloads.cost: None at run time: the choice is made when compiling. Each call is a direct call to the thunk of the chosen function, the same call C++ makes to that overload. There is no table and no dispatch, and nothing is checked while the program runs. At compile time the ranking runs once per call of an overloaded name (to measure).

verdicts_kept.verdict: 125: C++ members stay unsafe until an overlay entry vouches
verdicts_kept.how: Kept per function. An overload with no entry stays unsafe to call. An entry written `unsafe fn` carries its own `@safety` for its one function, and an entry that fits several functions or none is E5010, so a line never vouches for a function its writer did not name.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 131: C++ member lines go under their class
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. Entries for overloaded members (`fn new(width, height)`, `fn set_volume(level: f32)`) go under their `class` section. A top-level entry still names only a function outside any class.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 132: @ffi(const) on an entry
verdicts_kept.how: Kept per function. Each overload's entry says by itself whether that method only reads its object.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 146 and 147: `owns` at a call only for an `owns` parameter, and always there
verdicts_kept.how: Kept and used: the words at the call set which functions a call reaches, so `push(first)` and `push(owns second)` pick `const T&` and `T&&`. With only one of the two declared, the existing errors stay as they are (E3028).

verdicts_kept.verdict: 134: one L3015 per C or C++ function, naming every other call
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, with each function of an overloaded name counted as one function (to_verify).

verdicts_kept.verdict: 159: a constructor's argument takes no word
verdicts_kept.how: Not reached. It is about Ember's own `Name(…)` constructors. Whether an imported C++ `new` takes call words was open before this edit and stays open (notes).

decisions.title: How a C++ name with several functions reaches Ember, and which one a use takes
decisions.problem: C++ headers declare several constructors and overloaded methods and functions under one name, but Ember's own declarations have no overloading. The spec does not say what Ember names they get or how a call, an override or a function used as a value picks one. The compiler can work out the function from what the use supplies. Only where two still tie does it need a written word (`x as T`) or a refusal.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)   # Renderer(int, int)
r.draw(mesh)                           # draw(const Mesh&)
r.draw(hud)                            # draw(const Sprite&)
options.outcome: Compiles and calls the function C++ would call, among those Ember's own rules let the call reach (count, the words at the call, types; values checked after). The arguments' own types come first, then C++'s ranking. A call that reaches none is `E2020`, and one where two rank equal is `E2070`, each naming every function. An override or a value takes the one whose parameter types it has.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)
r.draw_Mesh(mesh)
r.draw_Sprite(hud)
options.outcome: Compiles. Each overload is its own Ember function, named from types the program never wrote, and the names change when the header renames a type.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "renderer.hpp":
    class Renderer:
        rename new(width, height) as sized
        rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh
        rename draw(sprite) as draw_sprite
# then: r = eng.gfx.Renderer.sized(1280, 720); r.draw_mesh(mesh)
options.outcome: Without the overlay every overload is skipped, and `r.draw(mesh)` is the 'skipped: overloaded' diagnostic. With it, the renamed calls compile, at the cost of a new `rename` form and one overlay line per overload.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. Speed is equal for all three options: a direct thunk call chosen when compiling. On safety, A lets a call reach only what Ember's own rules allow, so no C++ narrowing or int-to-bool conversion makes a function reachable. It also refuses a tie, and never lets a known value change which function runs. On readability, A reads like the header and like the C++ call, B's invented names read worst, and C makes every import longer. 2. Safety (C4): A refuses a call that two functions fit equally, so nothing is picked silently. 3. Compile time first (C5): all three are compile time. 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): the compiler works out the function from the arguments, and `x as T` is needed only where two still tie. 5. The ordinary program (C2): A leaves `m.set_volume(7)`, `Value.new(3)` and `b.append(count)` as written, while B and C add names or lines. 6. Consistency (C6): FFI-39b already picks a C++ constructor 'by arity and argument types', TYP-24's own-type-first tier is kept, the finder's option A promises 'calls the overload C++ would call', and TYP-26's exception gives its reason (principle 6).
decisions.departs_from_verdict: No verdict covers C++ overloads, so none is departed from. The choice narrows §I.6's non-goal 'function overloading' to Ember's own declarations, as TYP-26's existing exceptions already do for operator-interface implementations. It is recorded for the owner's later review.

owner_short.one_line: A C++ class with two constructors and two `draw(...)` overloads: what Ember calls them, and how a call picks one.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | header | declares `Renderer()`, `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)`, `draw(const Sprite&)` | four functions, two names |
| 2 | importer | keeps one Ember name per C++ name | `Renderer.new`, `r.draw` |
| 3 | compiler | at `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` keeps only the functions the call can reach (count, `ref mut`/`owns` at the call, types) | `Renderer(int, int)` |
| 4 | compiler | at `m.set_volume(7)`, with `set_volume(float)` and `set_volume(int)` both reached, ranks them as C++ does | `set_volume(int)` |
| 5 | compiler | a call that two functions still fit equally | refused when compiling, naming both |
owner_short.today: The spec does not say: Ember's 'no two functions of one name' rule, the 'skip what cannot be imported' rule and the base-constructor pick each give a different answer.
options: A: one Ember name per C++ name, and each call picks the function C++ would, among those Ember's rules let it reach: `Renderer.new(1280, 720)`, `r.draw(mesh)`
B: one name per overload, built from its types: `Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)`, `r.draw_Mesh(mesh)`
C: overloads are skipped until an overlay renames each one: `rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh`, then `r.draw_mesh(mesh)`
owner_short.recommendation: A: the code reads the way the header does, nothing extra is written, a call never reaches a function through a conversion Ember forbids, and a class with a C++ base already picks its base constructor this way.

decisions.title: How an overlay entry names one of several functions that share name, count and parameter names
decisions.problem: Overlay entries are matched by name, parameter count and parameter names, and the second entry for one name is refused. `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)`, or `push(const Job& job)` and `push(Job&& job)`, share all three, so no entry can say which one it vouches for. The compiler cannot know which function the writer meant, so only a written word or a refusal is left.

options.outcome: A parameter written with a type is written whole, as the import gives it (`owns job: Job` for `T&&`), and each entry fits exactly one function. Entries are matched and overridden per function. `fn set_volume(level)` fits both and is `E5010`, naming both, and so is a typed line that fits neither. If the header later adds an overload that an entry then fits, the build stops at that entry.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "mixer.hpp":
    extend Mixer:
        fn set_volume_f(level: f32):
            # SAFETY: set_volume(float) only stores the level
            unsafe:
                this.set_volume(level)
options.outcome: No entry can name either overload, so `fn set_volume(level)` is `E5010` and both stay unsafe to call. Vouching for one needs a wrapper with an invented name.
The entry makes both overloads safe. If the header later adds `set_volume(void* level)`, the package's own build adds its record line, and the new overload is vouched for without anyone reading it.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once: (c) fails safety. 2. Safety (C4): (a) and (b) vouch only for what is written; (c) lets an unread function become safe to call. 3. Compile time (C5): all three. 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): in (a) the type says which function the entry's facts are about, which is the entry's meaning; (b) forces a bookkeeping wrapper with an invented name. 5. The ordinary program (C2): (a) changes no line where count or names already tell functions apart, and adds one type only where they do not. 6. Consistency (C6): the parameter is Ember's own form (`[param_word] name: type`), as `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries already write types. Checklist 12 says to add the missing syntax rather than exempt the case.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: None. It keeps verdicts 125, 131 and 132 per function. It departs from two lead rulings, not verdicts. First, decisions.md §10 dropped types from class entries to keep 'one way to write an overlay line'; here a type is optional, in the language's own parameter form, needed only where names cannot single out a function. Second, ODR-149's one entry per name now counts per function.

owner_short.one_line: One overlay line for one of two C++ overloads that share their parameter name: `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)`, or `push(const Job& job)` and `push(Job&& job)`.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | header | declares `set_volume(float level)` and `set_volume(int level)` | same name, same count, same parameter name |
| 2 | overlay writer | writes `fn set_volume(level: f32)` and `fn set_volume(level: c_int)` | each line names one |
| 3 | compiler | checks each line against the header | each overload safe to call as its own line says |
| 4 | overlay writer | writes `fn set_volume(level)` instead | refused: it fits both, and the error names them |
| 5 | header, later | adds `set_volume(double level)` | a line that now fits two stops the build |
owner_short.today: An overlay line is matched only by name, parameter count and parameter names, and a second line for one name is refused, so no line can name one of these overloads.
options: a: the line writes the parameter whole, the way the import shows it: `fn set_volume(level: f32)`, `fn push(owns job: Job)`
b: no line can name one, so both stay unsafe to call unless a wrapper with a new name is written in the overlay
c: `fn set_volume(level)` covers both, and also covers any overload the header adds later, without anyone checking it
owner_short.recommendation: a: one extra type, only where the names cannot tell the overloads apart, and nothing is vouched for without being written.

repair:K21-cpp-overloads.notes:
Process: I used only Read and Grep. Nothing was run, counted, written or changed. The script measures the new text; I kept it shorter than the first answer by reusing the replaced words in the two `change` edits.

How this differs from the first answer:
- The FFI-12 sentence is gone. Matching an entry to one function now lives in the FFI-39b sentence, and FFI-30c's one-entry rule and `override` match entries per function.
- GRM-35's parameter line now carries the type and word the old sentence asked for but the grammar refused.
- The choice reaches overrides and values, not only calls.
- The two-tier ranking taken from TYP-24 is kept as the first tier, and C++'s own ranking now decides after it.
- Values are checked after the choice.
- The set is 'the functions a C++ header declares under one name', not 'declarations the import gives one name'.
- Changed outcomes: the first answer's Linux `seek(long)`/`seek(long long)` sibling, which was E2070, now compiles and calls C++'s choice for `int64_t`; `m.set_volume(7)` compiles.

Pre-existing holes, for the gap list and not reasons to repair this edit:
- S1-9: whether an imported C++ `new` takes call words. FN-2a (p05 131-132) says a constructor's argument takes no word; FFI-40 (p21 162) imports `T&&` as `owns x: T`. This is open with a single constructor too. Verdict 159 is about Ember's `Name(…)`.
- E1-7: an Ember class overriding two functions of one C++ overload set. TYP-26 still refuses the class's second `override fn visit`, with or without this edit. The override property makes a later fix natural.
- E1-9: receiver-const pairs (K47, J8-05). If K47 maps the object's rights to C++ `const`, C++'s ranking would take the non-const one for a changeable object.
- FFI-48's 'rename one in the overlay' cannot name one function, since `rename` takes a name (K47).

Residuals for the lead (codes and wording, not language):
- GRM-35 line 277, 'Contract words take the place of types', now reads as 'where no type is written'. A later in-place addition could say so.
- E2070's code-table row ('ambiguous interface method') should also cover C++ calls.
- An argument with no C++ form (an `Array[f32]` reaching `std::span<const float>`) is ranked by C++ only when two such functions remain; check it ranks as the type it reaches.
- On Linux an `i64` argument takes C++'s choice for `int64_t` (`long`), so a `long long` overload beside a `long` one cannot be reached from Ember; calls still never fail.
- Ember's own-type tier can pick a different overload from C++ for the same literal: `set(5)` with `set(int)` and `set(long long)` takes `long long`, since Ember's `int` is 64 bits.
- §I.6's non-goal 'function overloading' stays true of Ember's own declarations. I.6 is not an allowed rule here.

triage.evidence: FFI-30c (p16-ffi.md 221-222): 'a later file's `override` entry replaces an earlier file's for that name, and any other second entry for one name is `E5010` (ODR-149)'. GRM-35 (p16 268): '`override`, replacing an earlier overlay's entry for that name'. The first answer's FFI-12 sentence made entries per declaration and left both of these by name, so the question's own overlay was both accepted and E5010. Without the edit it is consistently E5010.

GRM-35 (p16-ffi.md 262): `overlay_param := IDENT [":" contract {contract}]`; line 277: 'Contract words take the place of types'. The first answer's sentence required 'the type before any contract word', which this grammar cannot parse (`Span[f32]`, `*mut c_int`), and a one-word type parses only as a contract word.

CLS-4 (p05-declarations.md 337): 'A method named like an inherited one replaces it'. FFI-39 (p21-annex-c.md 123-124): the trampoline passes on 'exactly the virtual methods it overrides (`override fn`)'. The edit let both `visit` import (TYP-26 exception) but decided only 'Every call'. Without the edit the base's two `visit` are E1030 (p04 867-868) or skipped (FFI-20a), so the class was refused, not open to type confusion.

FFI-12 (p16-ffi.md 322-323) refuses only an entry 'whose name, parameter count or parameter names do not match'. The first answer added typed entries and refused only one that 'still fits several'; `fn lerp(from: f64, to: f64, t: f32)` fits neither declaration and was not refused.

TYP-5 rule 12 (p04-types.md 92-96) converts a whole number 'where the compiler knows every value it can have fits that type'. The first answer ranked 'an exact type before a coercion as in [TYP-24]', counting that coercion, so `out.put(code)` ran `put(uint16_t)` for 200, `put(int8_t)` for -1, and was E2070 for 5.

The first answer's sentence reads 'Every call of a name…'. `pick = mx.mathx.clamp01` is not a call, and TYP-5 rule 10 (p04 88) converts 'a function or lambda', while this name stands for two. Without the edit the two `clamp01` are E1030 or skipped; with it the value is undecided, so an implementation could pick one silently.

The first answer's words were 'declarations'. A declare-then-define pair is two declarations of one C++ function with identical parameters, so a literal reading gives E2070. FFI-17 (p21 11-12) counts 'one thunk per imported function'.

The edit did not say whether `set_scale(int) = delete` takes part. FFI-20a (p16 162-164) skips what the importer cannot represent. If it is dropped, `t.set_scale(2)` runs `set_scale(double)` (LEX-16, p02 139-141), losing the header's refusal.

FN-2a (p05-declarations.md 131-132): '`return a` and a constructor's argument take no word'. FFI-40 (p21 162): '`T&&` as `owns x: T`'. Whether `Label.new(owns spare)` takes the word is undecided with a single `Label(Glyphs&&)` constructor too, so without the edit. The edit's choice only inherits it.

TYP-24 (p04-types.md 563-566): 'an untyped literal counting as its default type (`int`, `f64`)'. LEX-16 (p02 139-141) lets `7` take an integer or a float type. Under the first answer, `set_volume(7)` reached `c_int` and `f32` equally and was E2070, where C++ calls `set_volume(int)`.

FFI-8 (p16-ffi.md 173) maps `long` to `c_long` and `long long` to `i64`, and p15-stdlib.md 71 says the C names are aliases. On Linux both are `i64`, so under the first answer `b.append(count)` was E2070 and no Ember spelling reaches either function, so the message has no compiling line (checklist 9).
The same as S1-1: FFI-30c (p16 221-222) and GRM-35 (p16 268) still refuse or replace entries by name, against the first answer's FFI-12 sentence.

The same cause as S1-2, plus the word: the import gives `job: Job` and `owns job: Job` (FFI-40, p21 161-163), and `overlay_param` (p16 262) has no word before the name, so the `const T&`/`T&&` pair could never be named.

The first answer's exception, 'the declarations a C++ header's import gives one name', covers two header functions that an overlay's `rename … as draw` (GRM-35, p16 257) gives one name. Today that is E1030, as for C.

The same cause as S1-6: the edit decided calls only, and `sample(an.anim.smooth, 0.5)` uses the name as a value (TYP-5 rule 10, p04 88). Without the edit the two `smooth` are E1030 or skipped, so it is refused. With it, it is undecided.

TYP-26 (p04-types.md 867-868) refuses the Ember class's own second `override fn visit` with and without the edit, since the exception covers only the header's functions. FFI-39 (p21 121-125) says nothing of overload sets either way.

TYP-24 (p04 563-566) has two tiers, exact and coercion, and an upcast is a coercion (TYP-5 rule 8, p04 84-86). Under the first answer, `world.add(crate)` reached `add(const Body&)` and `add(const RigidBody&)` equally and was E2070, where C++ takes the nearer base.

FFI-48's row (p21-annex-c.md 90) and K47 (J8-05) hold the receiver-const pair. The two `root()` take no arguments and differ only in the object's `const`, which was undecided before the edit and is not decided by it.

causes.cause: An overlay entry was known by its name alone. It was matched, replaced by `override` and counted for the one-entry rule by name, in a grammar that writes only names and contract words. So no entry could single out one of several functions of a name, and none was refused for fitting none.

The function a use takes was chosen for calls only, by Ember's two-tier interface ranking applied with known values. That ranking did not reach overrides or functions used as values, and it lacked C++'s own ranking: literal kinds, nearer bases, deleted functions, and types that import alike.
The set was 'the declarations a C++ header's import gives one name'. That counted declarations, not functions, and included names an overlay gives as well as the header's own.

tests.name: K20_channel_of_any_error
tests.program:
import std.fs
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

fn page_size(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
    body = fs.read_to_string(path)?
    return Ok(body.len())

fn serve(path: String, failures: Sender[AnyError]):
    r = page_size(path)
    match owns r:
        Ok(n):
            println(f"{path}: {n} bytes")
        Err(e):
            failures.send(owns e).expect("the logger is gone")

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[AnyError](capacity=16)
    worker = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: serve(String("index.html"), tx))
    for e in rx:
        println(f"failed: {e}")
    worker.join()
tests.expected: with index.html missing: stdout `failed: <the io message>`; with it present: `index.html: <n> bytes`

from std.ffi import c_int

@layout(c)
struct Token:
    start: *u8         # points into the lexer's own copy of the source
    len: usize
    kind: c_int

# SAFETY: the declaration matches lexer.h
unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks, param(tokens, borrowed, count(cap), exclusive))
    safe fn lex_batch(ref mut tokens: MutSpan[Token], cap: usize) -> usize

fn main():
    batch: [Token; 256] = [Token(start=null[*u8](), len=0, kind=0); 256]
    n = lex_batch(ref mut batch)
    total: usize = 0
    for i in 0..n:
        total += batch[i].len
    println(total)
# C: size_t lex_batch(struct Token* tokens, size_t cap) writes up to cap tokens and reads none
holes.today: Compiles. `tokens` is a pointer whose contract is complete (borrowed, count(cap), exclusive), which FFI-10's list accepts (p16-ffi.md 59-61). It is mapped to `ref mut tokens: MutSpan[Token]` (p16 104-105; FFI-11 291, 296-298), and the witness `cap` leaves the callable signature (85-88). The raw-pointer refusal (82-84) looks only at a parameter's own type, as the repair itself says. The program is safe: C only fills the tokens, and Ember can read `start` only as a value and use it only in `unsafe` (p04-types.md 345-346).
holes.with_edit: E5002 at `safe fn lex_batch`, naming `Token.start`. It is a raw pointer held behind the parameter's pointer, which Ember may set (main fills the array before the call), and the `exclusive` contract lets C read as well as write it. No contract word says C only fills a counted buffer: `out` is defined for one value only (p16 301; p26-appx-h.md 1100, `param(p, out, one)`).
holes.what_goes_wrong: A correct program that compiles today is refused, with no safety gain. It is the answer's own sibling `lex_next` in batch form: the same pointers C made, handed to Ember and never read back. The edit accepts one token returned by value and refuses 256 tokens returned into a buffer, so the outcome depends on the shape the pointer travels in. That is principle 4, the argument the edit itself used against option B. The binding must become `unsafe fn` with an `@safety` that gives callers nothing to make true, plus a wrapper: the meaningless ceremony (C3) and longer binding (C2) the repair accepted as real in E1-1. The same happens to `backtrace(void** buffer, int size)` (a game engine's crash reporter, `MutSpan[*mut void]`), to `epoll_wait` (a Linux server's event loop; `struct epoll_event`'s `data` union holds `void* ptr`), and to any two-call enumeration (FFI-11b, p16 313-317) of structs holding pointers.
holes.fix_hint: Whether foreign code reads what it is given is the contract's to say, for a counted buffer as for one value: memory C only fills is inert, as an `out` slot is.

holes.today: Accepted. A capture-free function is accepted for a callback parameter (p16-ffi.md 400-401). Returning `ref_to_ptr` of a local is safe and keeps no view (p04-types.md 340-346), and E5042 covers only pointers into a copied parameter (p16 424-434). C reads 4,096 bytes from a dead stack slot (C++: a callback returning `&local`).
holes.with_edit: Undecided (E1-3 re-tested). The repaired words are about flow, "held, by value or behind a pointer, where Ember may set it and foreign code read it", and the callback's result is a raw pointer Ember sets and C reads. Read so, `decode_all` is E5002. The edit's own to_verify applies the same flow test to a callback type's slots ("The callback type's own `*mut void` parameter is set by C and read by Ember, so the new words do not reach it"), and by that test the result slot is reached. Its triage says the program is unchanged; read that way, C reads the dead slot as today.
holes.what_goes_wrong: An implementer cannot tell whether a raw pointer an Ember callback returns to C is covered. One reading closes this memory-corruption route from safe code. The other keeps it, though the edit's why_general says "Wherever such a pointer is held, no assertion of safety covers it". The same holds for a callback type whose result is a struct holding a raw pointer.
holes.fix_hint: The way a raw pointer flows decides in every slot a declaration's types reach, a callback's result included: Ember sets it, foreign code reads it.

holes.with_edit: The answer wants `lex_next` accepted and `current_target` refused, but the edited words, "where Ember may set it and foreign code read it", do not say which foreign code reads, or when. `current_target` is refused only if 'read' covers a later read by another function (`present`, not `current_target` itself). With that meaning, Ember's own Token copy can also be read later by foreign code it is handed to, so `lex_next` is refused too. With the narrower meaning (this call's foreign side), both are accepted.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Read one way for both, the words either bring back E1-1's needless refusal of the parser's lexer, or leave sibling 5's corruption route open. Telling them apart needs the distinction the words leave out: what C reads by itself (what it was given, and its own memory) versus Ember's own copy, which reaches C only through a later call that is checked there.

@layout(c)
struct Token:
    start: *u8
    len: usize
    kind: c_int

    @ffi(no_callbacks, param(tokens, borrowed, count(cap), exclusive))

rebreak-engineering:K07-raw-pointer-stru.notes:
Verdict: broken, by one medium hole the edit causes (H1). The repaired property fixes the first round's E1-1 for a copy, an `out` slot and a read-only view. It still refuses the same inert pointers when C hands them back by filling a counted buffer: a batch lexer, `backtrace`, `epoll_wait`, the two-call enumeration of FFI-11b. All of these compile today and are safe. No contract word can say "C only fills this buffer"; `out` exists for one value only (p16 301, p26 1100). FFI-11 is an allowed rule, so the fix lies inside the edit's own scope.

Re-tests of the first round:
- E1-2 (pre_existing): the repaired words now reach the C++ object, so it is fixed by this edit (to verify).
- E1-3 (pre_existing): now undecided rather than unchanged (H2). The edit's own to_verify applies a flow test to callback-type slots, and that test reaches a callback's result.
- E1-4: unchanged; pre_existing confirmed.
- E1-5: still open (H3, low).

Lower holes:
- H4: the words do not say which foreign code "reads". The answer's siblings 3 and 5 need two different scopes. The working reading is "what a call is given, and C's own memory".
- H5: verdict 136's plain-`fn` message still offers a `safe fn` line that the edit now refuses.

Checked and not holes:
- The binding cost reaches common libraries through `owns`/`ref mut` results of C structs holding pointers (SDL_Surface, cJSON, FFmpeg AVFrame). These are correct refusals of holes that exist today. The ordinary program then calls the library's wrapper.
- A `struct tm` binding is target-dependent. glibc and macOS have `tm_zone`, so `safe fn strftime(…, tm: Tm)` is E5002 there and compiles on MSVC. That is correct: glibc's %Z reads `tm_zone`. The message names the field.
- Reserved or user-data `void*` fields are refused, consistently with the existing top-level user-data refusal.
- An alternative tried and rejected: making writes to a pointer-holding struct's fields unsafe, instead of refusing the binding. Stale copies break it (a Token kept after C frees its source, then passed back), so the binding is the sound place to refuse.

Test hygiene: the answer's fixed program and siblings lack the `# SAFETY:` note above `unsafe extern "C":`. Without it the compiler gives W3012 (UNS-8, p09-memory.md 331-334). The tests here add the note. The E5002 for a struct with several raw-pointer fields should name every field in one diagnostic (verdict 134's lesson). The answer's message example names one.

Pre-existing gaps seen, outside the edit's raw-pointer reach, for the list:
- Function-pointer fields that C keeps and calls on its own thread (`struct sigaction`, `SDL_AudioSpec.callback`) have no thread contract.
- FFI-32 does not say whether a standard-layout C++ class's private members import as fields Ember can set. LLVM's StringRef is an example; the lifetime side is K09's.
- ODR-073 refuses a raw result at top level while a raw field in a by-value result is accepted. This asymmetry is kept and explained by the edit.

Nothing was run.

holes.program:
struct Pos:
    line: int
    col: int

struct Token:
    pos: Pos
    text: String

class Symbols:
    idents: Array[shares Token] = []

fn scan(ref mut syms: Symbols, words: Array[String]) -> int:
    width = 0
    col = 1
    for w in words:
        tok = Token(pos=Pos(line=1, col=col), text=copy of w)
        at = tok.pos
        if tok.text.len() > 2:
            syms.idents.push(shares tok)
        width = at.col + tok.text.len()
        col = width + 1
    return width

fn main():
    syms = Symbols()
    words = [String("fn"), String("parse"), String("x"), String("tokens")]
    println(scan(ref mut syms, words))
    println(syms.idents.len())
holes.today: Undecided (J5-06's gap). `at = tok.pos` names a part that has fields of its own, so it is a read-only view of bytes stored in `tok` (BRW-12 p07 194-200: only a part with no fields is copied). It is live at line 19 on the path that shares (BCK-2 p18 158-161: used at line 20). HEAP-3 (p09 61-62) moves `tok` into its block at line 19. Cost row 328 (p10) says nothing is allocated where no line says so.
holes.with_edit: Compiles and prints 18, then 2. Because `at` is live at the sharing point on the kept path, every token's value goes into a counted block where `tok` is given it (line 16), in every round: four blocks for two kept tokens. The rounds for `fn` and `x` allocate a block and free it on a path where no line that runs says `shares`. Every read of `tok` and `at` before line 19 goes through the block's address.
holes.what_goes_wrong: C++: `Pos* at = &tok.pos; if (keep) { auto s = std::make_shared<Token>(std::move(tok)); at = &s->pos; }` allocates only for kept tokens. C and Rust programmers point the pointer at the copy; they do not allocate first. Under the edit, a lexer's hot loop pays one malloc and one free per discarded token (to measure), with nothing on that path showing it. The only way to avoid it is a bookkeeping word (`at = copy of tok.pos`, C3). The J5-06 decision weighed only A (refuse) and B (block earlier). A third mechanism accepts every program B accepts and costs nothing on other paths: at the sharing line, each live view of the local's bytes follows them into the block. The compiler re-points it, much as a position is found again at each use: one add per live view, on the sharing path only. By C5 ('then the cheapest way') the parameters choose that mechanism. The earlier block is needed only where a view cannot be re-pointed (an address C keeps, verdict 114 fix 3). COST-5 (p10 353-354) also requires a cost-table row for an implicit cost, and the edit adds none.
holes.rule_lines: p09-memory.md 61-62 (HEAP-3 and the added sentence); p07-ownership.md 194-200 (BRW-12); p18-implementation.md 158-161 (BCK-2); p10-effects.md 328 (cost row), 353-354 (COST-5)
holes.fix_hint: State only the property (every view of the local's bytes live at a sharing line reaches them in the block after it) and let the compiler meet it the cheapest way: re-point the live views at that line; block earlier only where a view cannot be re-pointed.

import std.thread

struct Route:
    path: String
    handler: int

fn main():
    routes: Array[Route] = []
    for i in 0..3:
        routes.push(owns Route(path=String("/api"), handler=i))
    shared = thread_shared routes
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared shared: println(shared.len()))
    h.join()
holes.today: The spec says both. RC-1 (p08 106-108) lets `thread_shared` follow a local of this function, which becomes one of the owners. THR-1 (p11 70-74) and OWN-13 (p07 139-142) make line 11 E7017.
holes.with_edit: E7017 at line 11. The help cannot fold lines 8 to 10 into one making line, because a loop fills the list, and filling a value already made thread_shared is E7014 (p11 77-79). Two rewrites compile. (1) `shared = thread_shared copy of routes`: `Route` also needs `@derive(Clone)`, and the list and every `String` are copied, 1 + 3 allocations where Rust's `Arc::new(routes)` moves three words into one. (2) Move lines 8 to 10 into `fn load_routes() -> Array[Route]` and write `shared = thread_shared load_routes()`. THR-1 accepts that, because a call's result is 'a new value the callee made' (BRW-12 p07 200-201), and it puts the same bytes in the same 32-byte-header block line 11 would. So E7017 protects nothing here. An `Array` local has no header until a sharing line gives it its block (HEAP-3 p09 61-62). The refusal depends on spelling (a name against a call), not on what the value is.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A server builds its route table in a loop and hands it to its workers. That most ordinary startup code gets longer (a helper function, or a deep copy plus a derive) for no safety or cost reason. The decision's own parameters do not hold for this program. Parameter 5 says A's way is one line; that is false for a value built by a loop. Parameter 1 says A costs nothing; it costs a deep copy or a function. The class-header reason (OBJ-1 p08 63-69) applies only to a class object, whose header is fixed where it is made, and HEAP-3 already separates the two by that property ('A class object already has its block ... any other value is put in a block where it is made shared'). The same header question also applies to a class result, `thread_shared make_settings()` (E1-4), which A leaves accepted. So A does not avoid the mechanism it was chosen to avoid.
holes.rule_lines: p08-classes.md 107 (RC-1 as edited); p11-concurrency.md 70-79 (THR-1, E7017, E7014); p07-ownership.md 200-201 (BRW-12); p09-memory.md 61-62 (HEAP-3); p08-classes.md 63-69 (OBJ-1)
holes.fix_hint: Decide by HEAP-3's own property: a value whose block is made at the sharing line gets the header that line's word needs, whether a name or a call gives it; only a value whose header is already fixed needs creating shared (if this reads as a rule by type, it is the owner's question).

tests.name: lexer_position_view_hot_loop
tests.program:
struct Pos:
    line: int
    col: int

struct Token:
    pos: Pos
    text: String

class Symbols:
    idents: Array[shares Token] = []

fn scan(ref mut syms: Symbols, words: Array[String]) -> int:
    width = 0
    col = 1
    for w in words:
        tok = Token(pos=Pos(line=1, col=col), text=copy of w)
        at = tok.pos
        if tok.text.len() > 2:
            syms.idents.push(shares tok)
        width = at.col + tok.text.len()
        col = width + 1
    return width

fn main():
    syms = Symbols()
    words = [String("fn"), String("parse"), String("x"), String("tokens")]
    println(scan(ref mut syms, words))
    println(syms.idents.len())

rebreak-engineering:K06-sharing-a-local.notes:
Engineering lens. Every program in the answers and the nine sibling cases checks out as stated, for the orders the answer chose. Four holes are caused by the edit, all medium, so broken is true.

1. The earlier block costs more than C on paths that never share (lexer hot loop). E1-2 was triaged 'real' and kept as the price of accepting the view. But the decision weighed only A (refuse) and B (block earlier). A third mechanism, carrying the live views of the local's bytes into the block at the sharing line (re-pointing them), accepts the same programs. It costs nothing on other paths, and C5 picks it. It also removes holes 2 and 3.

2. S1-2 was refuted wrongly in part. The two-paths/two-arenas half of the round-1 hole was never answered. The triage's general claim ('in every program LT-4 accepts, the instance exists wherever the local is given a value') fails when an arena name is given a new instance in between.

3. An arena reset between the local's value and the sharing line: under the earlier block, the program is refused for a hidden reason or memory is corrupted.

4. J4-05's choice refuses `thread_shared` of a list or struct local. That value has no header yet, and THR-1 accepts the same bytes from a call (BRW-12). So E7017 there protects nothing, and the ordinary 'build a table in a loop, share it with workers' program needs a helper function or a deep copy. The class-object reason (OBJ-1) holds only for class objects, and the same header question applies to a class call result (E1-4), which A leaves accepted.

Pre-existing, re-tested and confirmed: S1-4, S1-6, E1-4, E1-5, E1-6.

Smaller points, not filed as holes:
(a) The outcome is labelled `decided` while both decisions are `made_by: parameters`. Under RULES D2 that is `decided_by_parameters`, which means nothing goes into the spec before the owner reviews it.
(b) '(a string's text)' assumes a String's text never sits inside the String itself. The spec does not fix String's layout, so a short-string layout that stores small text inline would make that example false.
(c) The cost claim 'a view into memory the local owns costs nothing' depends on each function's summary recording whether a view it returns points into the object's own bytes or into memory it owns. Otherwise every view a call gives must be assumed to point into the bytes, and pays the earlier block. EFF-1/EFF-4 carry summaries but do not name this fact.
(d) COST-5's missing row, already listed for the lead.

Nothing was run. Every expected output in tests is for the lead to confirm on the compiler.

holes.today: Compiles. `Task` is a `@layout(c)` value type (p16 59-61), and the raw-pointer refusal (82-84) speaks of `*T` only. `pool_release` coerces to `unsafe extern "C" fn(u32)` (p05 181-183: "an `unsafe fn` coerces only to an `unsafe` callable type"). Storing it is no unsafe operation: p09 266-270 lists calling through such a value, not making one, and p09 360 shows a safe function returning one. C then calls `pool_release(1000000)` and writes past the pool (C++: a job's completion pointer set to a function whose precondition nobody checked).
holes.with_edit: Unchanged. The edited words reach "a raw pointer". `finish` is a C function pointer, which FFI-56 itself calls unsafe to call (p16 590-596). Holding one where Ember sets it and C calls it is reached by no word. At the top level, FFI-21 (400-401) speaks only of capture-free Ember functions and `extern "C" fn` values; in a field nothing speaks at all.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Memory corruption from code with no `unsafe` in it (verdict 60). It is J8-08's property (a pointer safe code chose, which C uses unchecked) on the other kind of pointer. FFI-56 is one of the rules this edit touches.
holes.fix_hint: A pointer whose use safe code cannot check, a data pointer or a function unsafe to call, keeps the call unsafe when it is held where Ember may set it and foreign code use it.

holes.today: Likely compiles. The result is a `@layout(c)` value type (p16 59-61). The field is written as a safe callable type, and a call through an `extern "C" fn` is safe (p04 349-350, p06 264). FFI-56 says a function pointer from C, "a result" among them, imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn` (p16 590-592), but a hand declaration imports nothing, so no rule says whether its written safe type is refused. C scales 4,800 floats starting at one (C++: a plugin vtable entry called with `&one, 4800`).
holes.with_edit: Still undecided. The repaired words keep a struct C returns by value accepted, because what C hands back can be used only inside `unsafe` (p04 345-346). That premise is false for a safe-typed function pointer. The raw pointer passed to `process` is an argument of a call through a pointer held in the result, which is not 'held, by value or behind a pointer' in the words' sense.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Memory corruption from safe code. The written field type is a second, unlisted spelling of `@ffi(safe)` (`ember tcb` lists only `@ffi(safe)`, p21 214-215), and through it a raw pointer reaches C on the route this edit is meant to close.
holes.fix_hint: A function pointer C gives Ember is unsafe to call whatever type a declaration writes for it, unless an assertion that `ember tcb` lists says otherwise.

holes.today: Accepted. With `@ffi(std_function)` a `std::function` is "a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` ..., called as any other" (p21 67), with no condition on `A`. `Block` imports as a `@layout(c) struct` that Ember can build (p21 74-76), and `ref_to_ptr` is safe (p04 340-342). holes.with_edit: Undecided. The edit refuses "an overlay entry asserting such a function safe", but the `std_function` entry is a `type` entry that makes a value callable, not a function's own entry. The FFI-56 edit reaches `@ffi(safe)` typedefs only. The edit's statement that "all three assertion forms" now follow one rule misses this fourth form.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Memory corruption from safe code through a fourth way an overlay asserts foreign code safe. The same holds for a top-level `std::function<void(std::uint8_t*, std::size_t)>`.
holes.rule_lines: p21-annex-c.md 67 (FFI-17a), 74-76 (FFI-32); p16-ffi.md 82-84 (FFI-10, edited), 596-598 (FFI-56, edited); p04-types.md 340-342
holes.fix_hint: Every way a declaration or overlay makes foreign code safe to call meets the same raw-pointer property: a function, a member, a typedef, a `std::function` type.

Result: I found no high or medium hole caused by this edit. Every program in the answer and all seven sibling cases behave as the answer says under the rules plus the edit. The edit decides J8-08 and closes the use-after-free, race, double-free and forged-pointer routes in the matrix. It decides them when compiling, at the declaration.

Re-tests of the first round:
- E1-1: fixed. `lex_next`, `out` structs and read-only views are accepted.
- E1-2: correctly pre_existing. The repaired words now refuse it, because the object behind `this` is reached by "held ... behind a pointer".
- E1-3: correctly pre_existing. The result of a callback is neither held by value nor behind a pointer.
- E1-4: correctly pre_existing. The new clause speaks of what Ember may set. `ud` is a tagged number the compiler fills, and it is no address (p16 515-519).
- E1-5: stands as real and low (engineering). The XVI.4 rewrite must land with K46.

New gaps, all pre_existing and high (H1 to H3), for the list. Each is the J8-08 property on another kind of pointer or another way of asserting safety:
- H1: an unsafe C function pointer in a struct field that Ember sets and C calls. FFI-56 is an allowed rule.
- H2: a function pointer that C fills into a hand-declared struct field typed safe, which Ember then calls safely. It is a second, unlisted spelling of `@ffi(safe)`.
- H3: `@ffi(std_function)`, a fourth way of asserting safety (p21 67), which the edit's "all three forms" does not reach.

Soundness note for the lead: the E1-1 relaxation relies on "the parameter half refuses every safe way to hand them back". E1-3 (a callback's or an export's result) and H2/H3 are safe routes back to C. So a token pointer from `lex_next`, returned by an Ember callback after C has freed its source, is still a use-after-free. That is the same outcome as today, so it is pre_existing, but the relaxation is only fully sound once E1-3 is closed.

Wording note, low and not a hole: the edited FFI-56 says "a scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type, as for a `safe fn` ([FFI-10])". `Block` is a `@layout(c)` value type, so the PFN_mix_block refusal rests entirely on reading "as for a `safe fn`" as FFI-10's whole test, including 82-84, and not only its list at 59-61. I read it as deciding the case; a plainer cross-reference would remove the doubt.

Engineering observations, outside my lens, for the other breaker:
- tree-sitter's API (`ts_tree_root_node` accepted, but every `ts_node_*(TSNode self, …)` refused) and epoll (`epoll_ctl` and `epoll_wait`, whose `epoll_data_t` union imports with `void* ptr` and which the kernel never dereferences) both become `unsafe fn` plus wrappers under the edit. They are parsers and servers, the bar's ordinary programs.
- The answer's fixed J8-08 program has no `# SAFETY:` note on its `unsafe extern` block, so it gets W3012 (p09 331-335), as the spec's own examples do.

Union tests were left out: the spec gives no syntax for building a `@layout(c, union)` value (ODR-248, "as built").

Nothing was run. T1 to T21 are for the real compiler.

import std.thread

    hits: Array[String] = []
    fn record_hit() owns hits:              # a request logger keeping its own list of hits

holes.today: Undecided. FN-2a p05:132-133 lends `record_hit` to scope.spawn, which 'takes one', but nothing says what a task keeps of a lent function. Two readings are open. (a) The task uses the caller's own `record_hit`, as CLO-2 p06:245-247 treats a real variable ('a place that holds the function value counts as reaching every real variable it uses'). Then both tasks change `record_hit`, and THR-11 p11:390-396 gives E7007. (b) The task holds a copy of the function's words, and nothing sees one place.
holes.with_edit: The edit settles it on reading (b), and the program compiles with a data race. It says what the call keeps 'may not outlive h's state', a limit on how long it lives only. Its cost line says 'a callee that keeps them (an adapter, a scoped task) holds those same two words'. Its triage (cause 2) drops 'the caller's real variable' on purpose. Each task therefore runs `record_hit` through its own scope.spawn parameter, and CLO-18 p06:362-364 makes such a call 'a change of the place that holds it': two different places. The lifetime limit holds, because the scope ends before `record_hit` does. THR-11 finds no single place that two tasks change, so there is no E7007. Both tasks push onto the one `Array[String]` in `record_hit`'s state block at once. The parent calling `record_hit()` inside the block while a task runs is the same race. EFF-26 p10:141-143 ('changes every place its functions change') supports reading (a), so the edit leaves the program undecided at best, and its own model lets it through.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A data race in safe code. Two threads call `push` on one list with no lock. A reallocation frees the buffer the other thread is writing into, so memory is written after it is freed. In C++ terms: two std::threads given std::ref of one lambda whose captured vector both push_back onto. The same program written with `owns record_hit` is E3040, and with a lambda written in each call each task has its own list. Only the no-word loan shares the state. Writing the task as `scope.spawn(owns fn(): record_hit())` makes `record_hit` a real variable that the task uses, which E7007 does see. So two spellings of one program get opposite verdicts.
holes.rule_lines: Edited FN-2a p05:132-134 ('what the call keeps of it may not outlive h's state') and the edit's cost line ('holds those same two words'); CLO-18 p06:362-364; CLO-10 p06:275-278; THR-11 p11:387-396; THR-13 p11:135-139; EFF-26 p10:139-143; E7007 p17a:210
holes.fix_hint: A kept loan of `h` is `h` itself for every rule. A call through it changes `h` (CLO-18), so THR-11 sees two tasks, or a task and the parent, changing one place (E7007).

holes.program:
fn main():
    latencies = [12, 40, 7]                 # each request's time, in milliseconds
    count = 0
    fn note(ms: int) owns count:            # numbers the requests it has seen
        count += 1
        println(count, ms)
    latencies.iter().for_each(note)         # no word: lent
    note(99)                                # the caller's still
holes.today: FN-2a p05:132-134 lends `note` to for_each, and `note` is 'the caller's still'. The text does not say whether the callee works on `note` itself or on a copy of its two words. A loan of the caller's `note` reads as the first, which prints 1 12, 2 40, 3 7, 4 99.
holes.with_edit: The output depends on how big `note`'s state is. The edit's cost line says 'A loan gives the callee h's two words, {code, state}', and CLO-10 p06:278 lets 'a state of one word or less ... be kept in the state word itself, with no block'. With `owns count` (one int), for_each's `f` holds a copy of the count. Its calls change that copy, because CLO-18 makes a call a change of 'the place that holds it', which is for_each's own parameter. The copy ends with the call, and `note(99)` prints 1 99. With two captured ints (`owns count, owns total`) the state is a block both sides share, and `note(99)` prints 4 99. If the compiler instead follows the rule text, so that the change is `note`'s own, a loan of a one-word state must pass the address of `note`'s words. That is one more load per call (to measure), against the cost claim 'holds those same two words ... expected difference from C is zero'.
holes.what_goes_wrong: What a program does depends on a size the programmer never sees, adding a field to the captures changes the output, and a counter's changes are silently lost. That goes against principle 4 (one meaning for every type) and principle 7 (the code does what it says). In C++ terms: a lambda passed by value to std::for_each, whose mutable count is lost, but only when the captures fit in a pointer. If the compiler keeps the meaning instead, the edit's claim of zero cost does not hold.
holes.rule_lines: The edit's cost section and why_general ('A loan is the function `h` holds'); CLO-10 p06:275-281; CLO-18 p06:362-364; edited FN-2a p05:132-134
holes.fix_hint: A loan reaches `h` itself, never a copy of its words: a change a lent function makes to its own state is `h`'s for every state size, and the cost of reaching an inline state through `h`'s address is stated per call (to measure).

fn main():
    saved: Option[Config] = None
    default_cfg = Config(name=String("default"))
    fallback = fn() owns default_cfg => default_cfg    # gives its config away, so it runs once (`once fn`)
    cfg = saved.unwrap_or_else(fallback)                # no word: lent; the call hands `default_cfg` out
    spare = fallback()                                  # the caller's still: hands the same config out again

holes.today: It compiles, by one of two readings. FN-2a p05:132-134 lends a function from a variable to 'a standard-library function that takes one', and `unwrap_or_else` takes `[F: needs once fn() -> T]` (p13:72), so `fallback` stays 'the caller's still'. The callee's call uses it up in the callee's place (CLO-6a p06:315-318), so the caller's first `fallback()` is not E3040 (CLO-6 p06:312). Against that, CLO-6 p06:310 says 'A parameter that takes a once fn holds it'.
holes.with_edit: The same. `owns f: F` with `F: needs once fn() -> T` is 'a needs fn bound', so it is lent, and 'h is the caller's still'. The new limit, 'may not outlive h's state', does not cover a callee that uses the state up during the call.

In C++ terms: two std::unique_ptr built from one raw pointer. `Option.map`, `and_then`, `or_else` and `ok_or_else` (p13:68-79) do the same.
holes.fix_hint: A loan never lets the callee use up what the caller keeps: a function whose call uses it up (`once fn`) is lent to no parameter; it is handed over (`unwrap_or_else(owns fallback)`), E3028 without the word.

Verdict: broken. Hole 1 (high, this_edit) and hole 2 (medium, this_edit) both come from one choice in the repair. The repair makes a kept loan 'the function h holds', meaning a copy of h's two words held in the callee's own place, instead of h itself. Its only added limit is lifetime ('may not outlive h's state'), and it gives no rule for who may change the function's state.

Hole 1, a race. CLO-18 counts a call through a function value as a change of 'the place that holds it'. So two scoped tasks, or a task and the parent, that run one lent function changing its own state change two places as far as THR-11 can see, while in memory they change one state block. There is no E7007, and the program races. The classification: without the edit, what a task keeps of a lent function is undecided, and one reading (CLO-2's real variable) refuses it with E7007. The edit's model, cost line and triage choose the reading that lets it through. That is why I mark it this_edit, not pre_existing. The lead may weigh it against the answer's own claim that scope.spawn lending is 'the same as today'.

Hole 2, a lost change. CLO-10 lets a state of one word sit in the state word itself. A copy of the two words then copies the state, so a lent counter's changes are lost or kept depending on the state's size. If instead the compiler passes h's address, the claim of zero cost is false for such a state.

One fix covers both, as a property: a loan is h itself for every rule and every state size.

Hole 3 (high, pre_existing). A lent `once fn` given to Option/Result's `needs once fn` methods is used up by the callee while the caller keeps it, which gives a double free. Today's 'that takes one' reaches it in the same way. It is a new gap for the list.

The round-1 holes marked pre_existing were re-tested from their own programs: S1-4, S1-5, E1-5, E1-7 and E1-8 are all correctly pre_existing, and none was refuted. E1-5 still stands against the edit's own to_verify claim that `for_each(owns h)` is accepted, because STD-19 p15:316-317 says 'takes no word'. The repaired holes S1-1, S1-2, S1-3, E1-1, E1-2, E1-3 and E1-4 are closed by the parameter-declaration line.

Minor point, not a hole: the to_verify claim of E3026 for replacing `step = fn(): ticks += 1` while a scoped task holds it is not needed for safety. That old state owns nothing (only the address of `ticks`), so refusing it may be a needless refusal. I kept it as the edit's stated outcome.

holes.today: Line 16 takes a block from `pool` only on the rounds that run it, at most 8 in all. The making line names the instance and calls its `allocate` (ALC-1 p09 189-191; verdict 24). `em` and `p` are made after `pool`, so LT-4 is met. On those 8 rounds, `tag` (a name for a part, a view: BRW-12 p07 194-198) is used on line 17 after the sharing line, which is J5-06's gap. The pool's capacity is never at stake.
holes.with_edit: `tag` views bytes stored in `p` (the String's header), and on line 16 it is live at the point that shares it. So `p`'s value is in its block from line 13, every round, whether the round shares or not. The block must be the one line 16 names, from `pool`: a block from `Global` moved into `pool` at line 16 would move what `tag` reaches, which the sentence rules out. On a round that does not share, `p` ends at the end of the round and its block goes back to `pool`. A FixedArena's `deallocate` does nothing (ALC-1 p09 205-207; verdict 107 (b): 'everything is freed together when the manager is cleared or ends'). So the rounds that never share use up the pool, and the FixedArena panics on exhaustion (ARN-4 p09 120-124) at line 13, a line that names no arena. With a growing `Arena`, the arena instead grows by one block per round for as long as the loop runs (the rate is to measure).
holes.what_goes_wrong: A correct game loop that keeps at most 8 particles in a fixed pool stops, or with a growing arena grows without bound. The cause is an allocation that no line which runs asks for. C++ terms: `std::allocate_shared(pool, ...)` for every particle just in case, from a monotonic buffer resource that never reuses memory. The repair's cost text says such a path pays 'that allocation and its free'. With a manager that frees nothing one by one, there is no free. It also breaks row 328 (p10): 'nothing is copied or allocated where no line says so'.
